q: A utility contracts to buy all the fuel oil its plant requires at 2 cents per gallon, estimating 1 million gallons a year. When the market price rises to 6 cents, the utility starts burning oil instead of natural gas, which it had used before, so that it can sell its spare gas at a profit. Its oil requirements jump to 2.5 million gallons. What is the most likely result?
o: The utility wins, because a requirements contract lets the buyer alone decide how much it needs.
The seller wins only if the contract set a maximum quantity, since § 2-306 has no ceiling of its own.
The utility wins, because it actually burned all 2.5 million gallons at its own plant during the year.
The contract is void, because a fixed price far below the market price is unconscionable.
The seller wins, because requirements inflated to profit from the market aren't requirements in good faith.
oe: The buyer's needs must be in good faith and not unreasonably disproportionate.
Section 2-306(1) supplies the limits even without a stated maximum.
Actual use doesn't make requirements generated in bad faith legitimate.
A favorable fixed price isn't unconscionable. The problem is the buyer's conduct.

Correct. Requirements must be those "as may occur in good faith" (§ 2-306(1)). Switching fuels to profit from the price difference is the kind of conduct Orange & Rockland v. Amerada Hess held to be bad faith, and the demand also far exceeds the estimate.
topic: Tier 2 · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Requirements: increase to exploit the market

q: Under a six-month contract requiring delivery by the 1st of each month, the buyer emails the seller in February: "No need to rush; deliveries by the 15th are fine for the rest of the contract." Relying on that email, the seller rebooks its production line and gives the 1st-to-14th slots to another customer under a new contract it can't change. In April, the buyer emails that it will now insist on delivery by May 1. What is the most likely result?
o: The buyer may retract, because estoppel doesn't apply to contracts for the sale of goods.
The seller wins, but only because the buyer's February email was a signed writing.
The buyer may retract, because it gave the seller reasonable notice well before the May 1 delivery.
The buyer may retract, because a waiver given without consideration can be withdrawn at any time.
The buyer probably can't retract, because the seller materially changed position in reliance.
oe: Article 2 is supplemented by estoppel principles (§ 1-103(b)), and § 2-209(5) builds reliance into the waiver rule.
The writing matters for any no-oral-modification clause, not for retraction under § 2-209(5).
Reasonable notice isn't enough when the other party has materially changed position in reliance.
Waivers don't require consideration. The obstacle is reliance.

Correct. A waiver affecting an executory portion of the contract may be retracted by reasonable notice "unless the retraction would be unjust in view of a material change of position in reliance on the waiver" (§ 2-209(5)).
topic: Tier 2 · Course of performance, waiver & estoppel (§ 1-303) — Waiver retraction blocked by reliance

q: Which of the following is NOT "goods" under § 2-105?
o: Shares of stock in a publicly traded corporation.
A machine to be specially manufactured for the buyer.
The unborn calves of a rancher's herd.
Growing crops.
Timber to be cut under a contract with a landowner.
oe: Correct. Goods exclude "the money in which the price is to be paid, investment securities (Article 8) and things in action" (§ 2-105(1)).
Goods include specially manufactured goods (§ 2-105(1)).
Goods include "the unborn young of animals" (§ 2-105(1)).
Growing crops are goods (§ 2-105(1)).
Timber to be cut is goods whether the buyer or the seller severs it (§ 2-107(2)).
topic: Tier 3 · Scope, goods & merchants (§§ 2-102, 2-105, 2-107) — What is NOT goods

q: Janice orders 100 red guitar straps from Floyd's Gear, F.O.B. Floyd's shop. Floyd ships 100 green straps by a reputable carrier and notifies Janice. A flash flood destroys the shipment in transit before Janice sees it. Who bears the loss?
o: Floyd, but only if the wrong color of the straps was what caused the loss.
Floyd, because a nonconforming shipment leaves the risk with the seller.
Janice, because in an F.O.B. seller's-shop contract risk passes on delivery to the carrier.
Janice, unless she rejects the straps after she has had a chance to inspect them.
The carrier, because the goods were in its custody when the flood destroyed them.
oe: Section 2-510(1) doesn't require any causal link between the nonconformity and the loss.

Correct. Where a tender or delivery so fails to conform that the buyer could reject it, the risk stays on the seller until cure or acceptance (§ 2-510(1)). Green straps are a nonconforming delivery, so the F.O.B. term never shifted the risk.
That rule in § 2-509(1)(a) applies only when there is no breach. Section 2-510(1) overrides it for a nonconforming tender.
A buyer can't inspect destroyed goods, and she doesn't need to. The nonconformity alone keeps the risk on the seller.
The carrier's liability doesn't settle the risk between buyer and seller.
topic: Tier 1 · Risk of loss & identification (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510) — Nonconforming goods in a shipment contract

q: Before buying an X3000 HVAC system, a building manager reads the maker's brochure, which states "300,000 BTU/hr output." The dealer's salesperson also says, "You'll be thrilled with it." The unit delivers 210,000 BTU/hr, and the manager isn't thrilled. Which statements are express warranties that the dealer made?
o: Only the salesperson's comment, because the brochure was the maker's statement, not the dealer's.
Both statements, because each was made to induce the manager to buy the system.
Neither, because output ratings in brochures are always understood to be estimates.
Neither, because the brochure wasn't signed by anyone at the dealership.
The brochure's output figure, if it was part of the bargain, but not the salesperson's comment.
oe: The salesperson's comment is puffing. When a dealer uses the maker's brochure to sell, its figures can become part of the dealer's bargain.
"You'll be thrilled" is sales talk, not a factual affirmation.
A specific BTU rating is a measurable fact.
Express warranties don't require a signature.

Correct. A specific output figure the buyer read before buying is an affirmation of fact that can become part of the basis of the bargain. "You'll be thrilled" is commendation (§ 2-313(2)). See Problem 3-7.
topic: Tier 1 · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Brochure vs. sales talk

q: The Count buys a grandfather clock from Telly's Antiques, a retail antiques store. The Count pays the full price, and the signed sales slip says "Title passes to Buyer upon payment." Telly says, "It's yours. Leave it here in the back room and pick it up whenever you like." Two days later, before the Count comes for it, a flood destroys the store and the clock. Who bears the loss?
o: The Count, because title passed to him when he paid.
The Count, because the clock was identified to the contract when the contract was made.
The Count, because the seller tendered the clock when it said he could pick it up at any time.
Telly's Antiques, because a merchant seller keeps the risk until the buyer receives the goods.
None of the above.
oe: Risk of loss under § 2-509 doesn't follow title. The title clause decides ownership, not who bears casualty losses.
Identification gives the buyer a special property and an insurable interest (§ 2-501). It doesn't shift the risk of loss.
Tender passes risk only when the seller is not a merchant. Telly's is a merchant, so the rule is receipt, not tender.

Correct. Under § 2-509(3), when the seller is a merchant and the goods are not shipped or held by a bailee, risk passes only on the buyer's receipt, meaning physical possession (§ 2-103(1)(c)). Passing of title and payment don't move risk; Article 2 deliberately separates risk from title.
One of the other choices is correct: Telly's Antiques, because a merchant seller keeps the risk until the buyer receives the goods.
topic: Tier 1 · Risk of loss & identification (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510) — Merchant seller; title and payment irrelevant

q: Two merchants orally agree on a sale of $12,000 of lumber. The next day, the seller sends the buyer a signed confirmation stating the quantity and price, and the buyer receives it that day. The buyer sends a written objection 12 days after receiving it, then refuses the lumber, raising the statute of frauds. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The seller wins only if the buyer, not the seller, is the one who sent the confirmation.
The buyer wins, because it sent a written objection to the confirmation.
The seller wins automatically, because the confirmation proves that a contract was made.
The statute is no defense, but the seller must still prove the contract was made.
The buyer wins, because it never signed anything, and the statute protects the party sued.
oe: The rule binds the recipient. It doesn't matter which side sent it.
The objection came after the 10-day period.
The confirmation removes the statute-of-frauds defense but isn't conclusive proof of a contract.

Correct. Between merchants, a written confirmation sufficient against the sender satisfies § 2-201 against a recipient who doesn't object within 10 days after receipt (§ 2-201(2)). Satisfying the statute only removes the defense. The seller still must prove the contract existed (§ 2-201 cmt. 3).
Section 2-201(2) is designed for a recipient who hasn't signed.
topic: Tier 3 · Statute of frauds (§ 2-201) — Merchant confirmation; objection too late

q: A farmer tells a seed dealer she needs a corn variety that will mature in her short northern growing season and asks the dealer to pick one. The dealer picks a variety, and the farmer signs a contract with a conspicuous clause: "SELLER EXCLUDES THE IMPLIED WARRANTY OF MERCHANTABILITY." The corn is healthy but needs a longer season and doesn't mature before frost. Which claim, if any, survives?
o: Neither, because healthy seed is merchantable.
Neither, because the clause excluded all implied warranties.
Fitness for a particular purpose, because the clause excludes only merchantability.
Merchantability, because a disclaimer of merchantability is unenforceable in a sale to a farmer.
Both, because the dealer selected the seed.
oe: Being merchantable doesn't defeat a separate fitness claim.
It names only merchantability. To exclude fitness, a conspicuous writing must address it, generally or specifically.

Correct. The clause meets § 2-316(2) for merchantability, but it doesn't purport to exclude fitness, and nothing else does. The dealer knew the purpose and the farmer relied on its selection, so § 2-315 applies.
The disclaimer satisfies § 2-316(2), so merchantability is excluded.
Selection supports fitness, but merchantability was effectively disclaimed.
topic: Tier 1 · Warranty disclaimers (§ 2-316) — Merchantability disclaimed; fitness survives

q: A written contract might include any of the following clauses. Which one, standing alone, would most clearly bar evidence of a consistent additional term agreed to orally before signing?
o: "This Agreement may not be modified or amended except by a writing signed by both parties."
"This Agreement shall be governed by and construed under the law of the State of Delaware."
"This Agreement represents the final agreement of the parties with respect to its subject matter."
"This Agreement is the complete and exclusive statement of the terms of the parties' agreement."
"Seller disclaims all implied warranties, including the implied warranty of merchantability."
oe: That's a no-oral-modification clause. It governs later changes, not prior terms.
A choice-of-law clause says nothing about integration.
A final writing bars contradiction, but without more it can still be supplemented by consistent additional terms.
Correct. A finding that the writing was intended as "a complete and exclusive statement of the terms of the agreement" is what bars consistent additional terms under § 2-202(b). See Problem 5-11.
That's a disclaimer, not an integration clause.
topic: Tier 2 · Parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) — Which clause creates a complete integration

q: Miss Piggy tells a hardware-store clerk that she needs paint for the inside of her swimming pool. The clerk suggests a pool epoxy, but Miss Piggy insists, "No, I want ParisMatte Interior Eggshell, my favorite brand." She buys it, paints the pool, and the paint peels within a week. Which statement is most accurate?
o: She has a merchantability claim, because paint that peels within a week isn't fit for any purpose.
Probably neither claim succeeds, because she didn't rely on the store and pool use isn't ordinary.
She has both claims, because the store is a merchant that deals in paint and knew her purpose.
She has no claims, because implied warranties never attach to brand-name goods the buyer selects.
She has a fitness claim, because the store knew exactly why she wanted the paint when she bought it.
oe: Merchantability is measured by the goods' ordinary purposes, not by an unusual use the buyer chose.

Correct. The fitness warranty requires the buyer's reliance on the seller's skill or judgment (§ 2-315). When the buyer insists on a particular brand, there's no reliance (§ 2-315 cmt. 5). Merchantability measures fitness for the ordinary purposes of interior paint, and pool use isn't one of them.
Merchant status supports merchantability, but the paint was fit for its ordinary use, and the fitness claim fails for lack of reliance.
Brand-name goods carry implied warranties. Insisting on a brand defeats only the reliance element of fitness.
Knowledge of the purpose isn't enough. The buyer must also rely on the seller to select the goods, and she overrode the clerk.
topic: Tier 1 · Implied warranties (§§ 2-314, 2-315) — Buyer insists on a brand: no reliance

q: A law firm upgrades its equipment and sells its five surplus laser printers to a local school. A tech company sues the school, claiming the printers' firmware infringes its patent. Which warranty, if any, did the law firm give the school?
o: The warranty against infringement only, because the claim concerns a patent.
Both the warranty of title and the warranty against infringement, because every seller gives both.
Only the warranty of title, because the firm doesn't regularly deal in printers.
No warranty at all, because the printers were used office equipment.
The implied warranty of merchantability, which covers infringement claims.
oe: The law firm doesn't make the infringement warranty, though it does make the title warranty.
The infringement warranty requires a merchant regularly dealing in goods of the kind.

Correct. Every seller warrants title (§ 2-312(1)), but the warranty against infringement applies only when "the seller is a merchant regularly dealing in goods of the kind" (§ 2-312(3)). A law firm doesn't deal in printers.
The title warranty applies to used goods.
Merchantability requires a merchant with respect to goods of that kind, and it doesn't address infringement.
topic: Tier 1 · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-403) — Infringement warranty needs a regular dealer

q: A contract provides that 30 crates of tile will be delivered "C.O.D." When the truck arrives, the buyer insists on opening the crates before paying. The driver refuses. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The buyer must pay first, but paying isn't acceptance, so it can still reject.
The buyer must pay, and by paying it gives up its right to inspect the tile.
The buyer may refuse to pay until it inspects, because the right to inspect can't be waived.
The driver must allow inspection, because C.O.D. describes only how payment is made.
Once the buyer pays, it has accepted the tile and can no longer reject it.
oe: Correct. Under a C.O.D. term, the buyer isn't entitled to inspect before payment unless otherwise agreed (§ 2-513(3)(a)). Payment required before inspection doesn't constitute acceptance or impair the buyer's right to inspect or its remedies (§ 2-512(2)).
The buyer keeps the right to inspect after payment.
The right to inspect before payment applies "unless otherwise agreed," and a C.O.D. term is such an agreement.
C.O.D. means payment on delivery, and § 2-513(3)(a) bars inspection before payment.
Section 2-512(2) says payment before inspection isn't acceptance.
topic: Tier 2 · Tender, inspection, acceptance & payment — C.O.D.: pay first, then inspect

q: Worried about a buyer's finances, a seller phones the buyer's purchasing manager, says it needs assurances, and stops shipping. The buyer doesn't respond. Three weeks later, the seller cancels the contract. The buyer sues. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The buyer wins only if it can prove that it was solvent the whole time.
The seller is protected, because reasonable grounds for insecurity justify cancellation.
The seller is in a weak position, because the demand should have been made in a record.
The seller is protected, because the buyer failed to respond within a reasonable time.
The seller is protected, because three weeks is a reasonable time to respond to a demand.
oe: The seller's own procedural failure is the main problem, whatever the buyer's finances.
Reasonable grounds justify a demand and suspension, not immediate cancellation.

Correct. Section 2-609(1) lets a party with reasonable grounds "demand in a record" (in writing) adequate assurance. Some courts excuse an informal demand when it is clear, but a phone call followed by quick cancellation is risky, and the seller may itself be the breaching party.
Treating silence as repudiation depends on a justified demand made the way § 2-609 requires.
The timing rule applies only after a proper demand.
topic: Tier 2 · Insecurity & repudiation (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Demand made only by phone

q: A contract calls for a seller to ship 2,000 cases of olive oil on a named ocean carrier from a particular port. Before shipment, that carrier goes out of business, but another reputable carrier at the same port can carry the goods on a similar schedule at a similar cost. The seller ships on the substitute carrier. Must the buyer accept the tender?
o: No, because the agreed carrier's failure excuses the seller from performing at all.
Yes, because a commercially reasonable substitute carrier must be tendered and accepted.
No, because the seller first had to try to get the original carrier to resume service.
No, because the contract named a specific carrier, so shipping on any other one is nonconforming.
Yes, but only if the buyer agreed in writing to the change of carrier before shipment.
oe: Excuse isn't available when a reasonable substitute exists. Substitute performance is required.
Correct. Where "an agreed type of carrier becomes unavailable ... but a commercially reasonable substitute is available, such substitute performance must be tendered and accepted" (§ 2-614(1)).
The statute asks only whether a commercially reasonable substitute is available.
Section 2-614(1) requires acceptance of a commercially reasonable substitute.
Section 2-614(1) needs no agreement.
topic: Tier 2 · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-615) — Substituted performance

q: Statler is selling his used pontoon boat to Waldorf. Statler says: (1) "She's the finest boat on the lake." (2) "She's worth at least $40,000." (3) "The hull is aluminum, and the motor has 300 hours on it." (4) "You'll be the envy of the marina." The motor actually has 1,900 hours. Which statement created an express warranty?
o: Statement (3) only.
Statements (1) and (3).
Statements (2) and (3).
All four statements.
None, because Statler isn't a merchant.
oe: Correct. A specific, verifiable affirmation of fact about the goods is an express warranty (§ 2-313(1)(a)). Statements (1) and (4) are commendation, and statement (2) is "an affirmation merely of the value of the goods," which creates no warranty (§ 2-313(2)).
"Finest boat on the lake" is general praise, or puffing.
An affirmation merely of value is not a warranty under § 2-313(2).
Only the specific factual statement is a warranty. The others are opinion, value, or praise.
Any seller can make an express warranty. Merchant status is irrelevant under § 2-313.
topic: Tier 1 · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Fact vs. value vs. puffing

q: Rosita, a nurse, agrees to sell her personal kayak to Zoe for $700. Rosita says, "I'll have it on my driveway for you starting tomorrow at noon." That night, before noon the next day, the kayak is stolen from Rosita's locked garage without either party's fault. Zoe hasn't paid. What is the most likely result?
o: Rosita must deliver a comparable kayak or pay Zoe damages for nondelivery.
The answer depends on whether Rosita is a merchant with respect to kayaks, which a court will presume she is.
Zoe must pay, because a non-merchant seller passes the risk as soon as the contract is made.
Zoe must pay, because Rosita had already told her when and where to pick up the kayak.
The loss falls on Rosita, and neither party owes the other anything further.
oe: The contract was for this identified kayak. Its loss without fault before risk passed avoids the contract under § 2-613, so Rosita isn't in breach.
There is no presumption of merchant status. And even for a non-merchant, risk had not passed because there was no tender yet.
A non-merchant passes risk on tender, not on contracting. Rosita had not yet made the kayak available.
Notice of a future pickup time isn't tender. Tender requires the goods to be actually held at the buyer's disposition.

Correct. A non-merchant seller passes risk on tender (§ 2-509(3)), and tender requires putting and holding the goods at the buyer's disposition (§ 2-503(1)). That hadn't happened yet. The kayak was identified when the contract was made and was lost without fault before risk passed, so § 2-613 avoids the contract.
topic: Tier 1 · Risk of loss & identification (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510) — Non-merchant seller; loss before tender

q: Big Bird runs a commercial greenhouse. For years he has bought supplies from Oscar's Garden Wholesale, whose sales rep has toured the greenhouse and knows Big Bird grows only orchids. Big Bird phones in an order: "Send me whatever fertilizer you think is best for my plants." Oscar's sends a fertilizer that works well for most plants but is known to scorch orchids. Has Oscar's made a fitness warranty?
o: No, because a fitness warranty arises only when the seller makes some affirmation of fact.
Yes, but only because Big Bird and Oscar's are both merchants dealing in garden supplies.
Yes, because Oscar's had reason to know both the particular purpose and Big Bird's reliance.
No, because the fertilizer works well for most plants and so was merchantable for ordinary use.
No, because Big Bird never told Oscar's that the fertilizer was for orchids when he ordered.
oe: That describes an express warranty. Fitness is implied from the circumstances.
Section 2-315 applies to any seller and any buyer.
Correct. The seller need only have "reason to know" the particular purpose and the buyer's reliance (§ 2-315). Past dealings and knowledge of the buyer's business can supply it (§ 2-315 cmt. 1).
The two warranties are separate. Goods can be merchantable and still unfit for the buyer's particular purpose.
Section 2-315 doesn't require the buyer to state the purpose expressly. Reason to know is enough.
topic: Tier 1 · Implied warranties (§§ 2-314, 2-315) — Fitness: reason to know without being told

q: Rosita, a dressmaker, visits a fabric wholesaler and handles a swatch cut from a bolt of silk charmeuse. She orders 300 yards "like this." The silk delivered is noticeably thinner and coarser than the swatch. The wholesaler says it never said anything about the weight or feel of the fabric. Which statement is most accurate?
o: A warranty arose, but only if the wholesaler intended the swatch to be a warranty.
Only an implied warranty of merchantability arose, because samples are covered by § 2-314.
The wholesaler made an express warranty that the whole delivery would conform to the sample.
No warranty arose, because Rosita could have tested the fabric herself.
No warranty arose, because the wholesaler made no oral or written statement about the fabric.
oe: The seller doesn't need to intend to make a warranty (§ 2-313(2)).
Samples create express warranties under § 2-313. Merchantability may also apply, but the sample warranty is the stronger claim.

Correct. "Any sample or model which is made part of the basis of the bargain creates an express warranty that the whole of the goods shall conform to the sample or model" (§ 2-313(1)(c)). No words are needed.
The buyer's chance to inspect doesn't defeat a warranty by sample.
A sample speaks for itself. Section 2-313(1)(c) requires no affirmation in words.
topic: Tier 1 · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Warranty by sample

q: On February 1, Statler and Waldorf contract for 1,000 sacks of oats, delivery on March 15, at a price "to be agreed at delivery." On February 1, oats sell for $7 a sack. On March 15, the market price is $12 and rising. Statler tenders and demands $15. Waldorf refuses, and they never agree. Assuming they intended to be bound, what price term governs?
o: $7, the market price when the contract was made.
$15, because the seller sets the price when it is left open.
A reasonable price at the time for delivery, likely around $12.
There's no contract, because the parties never agreed on the price.
None of the above.
oe: The gap filler looks to the time for delivery, not the time of contracting.
A price left to be agreed isn't one the seller fixes.
Correct. When the price is left to be agreed and the parties fail to agree, the price is "a reasonable price at the time for delivery" (§ 2-305(1)(b)). See Problem 4-3(a).
Section 2-305(1) saves the contract if the parties intended to be bound.
One of the other choices is correct: A reasonable price at the time for delivery, likely around $12.
topic: Tier 2 · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Price "to be agreed"; failure to agree

q: A plumber contracts to buy $40,000 of standard pipe fittings for a sewer project he has agreed to build for the town of Microville. Before delivery, Microville cancels the project. The fittings are standard items the plumber could use on other jobs. The plumber claims he is excused because his purpose has been frustrated. What is the most likely result?
o: Not excused, because losing his own customer is a risk the plumber bore.
Excused, because the only reason he bought the fittings no longer exists.
Excused under § 2-613, because the fittings can no longer be used as he intended.
Excused under § 2-615, because the town's cancellation of the project was unforeseen.
He can't raise frustration, because Article 2 doesn't recognize it.
oe: Correct. Frustration of purpose, a common-law doctrine that supplements Article 2 through § 1-103(b), requires that the principal purpose be substantially frustrated by an event whose non-occurrence was a basic assumption of the contract. A buyer's loss of its own customer is ordinarily a risk the buyer assumes. See Problem 6-8(a).
Frustration is narrow. The loss of a downstream contract usually isn't enough, especially for standard goods.
Section 2-613 concerns casualty to identified goods, which hasn't occurred.
Section 2-615 excuses sellers, and nothing makes the plumber's performance, which is paying, impracticable.
Article 2 is supplemented by the common law of excuse under § 1-103(b).
topic: Tier 2 · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-615) — Frustration of purpose

q: Midway through a fixed-price contract to supply aluminum cans, the seller, whose costs haven't changed, learns that the buyer has no other supplier able to meet its summer production schedule. The seller announces it will stop shipping unless the buyer agrees to a 20% price increase. The buyer agrees in a signed writing, then sues to recover the extra 20%. What is the most likely result?
o: The seller wins, because modifications under Article 2 are binding without any consideration.
The buyer wins, because the increase was extracted without a legitimate commercial reason.
The buyer wins, because the seller gave no new consideration in exchange for the higher price.
The seller wins, because the buyer agreed to the increase in a signed writing it could have refused.
None of the above.
oe: True, but they must still be made in good faith.

Correct. A modification needs no consideration (§ 2-209(1)), but it must be made in good faith, and "the extortion of a 'modification' without legitimate commercial reason is ineffective" (§ 2-209 cmt. 2). This is the Roth Steel point.
Section 2-209(1) eliminates the consideration requirement. The defect is bad faith.
A signed writing satisfies form requirements but doesn't cure bad faith.
One of the other choices is correct: The buyer wins, because the increase was extracted without a legitimate commercial reason.
topic: Tier 2 · Modification (§ 2-209) — Bad-faith price demand

q: Mr. Snuffleupagus takes home a $2,400 television from a store under a written deal that lets him use it for 14 days and pay only if he decides to keep it. On day 3, before he has decided, lightning strikes his house and destroys the television. Must he pay?
o: No, but only if he notifies the store of the loss before the 14 days run out.
Yes, because the television was in his possession and control when it was destroyed.
Yes, because this is a sale or return, which puts the risk on the buyer during the trial.
Yes, because the seller is a merchant and the buyer had already received the goods.
No, because the risk stays with the seller until he approves the purchase.
oe: The risk was on the seller regardless. No notice condition applies.
Possession during a trial period doesn't pass the risk in a sale on approval.
A sale or return is for goods delivered primarily for resale. This TV was delivered for the buyer's own use, so it's a sale on approval.
The merchant receipt rule in § 2-509(3) is subject to § 2-327, which keeps the risk on the seller until approval.

Correct. When goods are delivered primarily for use and may be returned even though they conform, the deal is a sale on approval (§ 2-326(1)(a)). Risk of loss and title don't pass until the buyer accepts (§ 2-327(1)(a)), and using the goods consistently with the trial isn't acceptance.
topic: Tier 1 · Risk of loss & identification (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510) — Sale on approval

q: After an oral agreement between two merchants, the buyer receives a signed letter from the seller: "Thank you for our discussion about the lumber. We look forward to doing business with you." The letter states no quantity. The buyer doesn't object. Can the seller use the letter to satisfy the statute of frauds against the buyer?
o: Yes, because both parties are merchants, and between merchants any signed letter will do.
Yes, because the missing quantity term can be filled in by the parties' testimony at trial.
Yes, because the buyer received the letter and didn't send a written objection within 10 days.
No, because a confirmation satisfies the statute only if it is signed by both of the parties.
No, because the letter doesn't indicate that a contract was made and states no quantity.
oe: Merchant status is necessary but not sufficient.
A writing that omits quantity can't support enforcement under § 2-201(1).
The 10-day rule applies only to a confirmation sufficient against the sender.
A confirmation need be signed only by the sender.

Correct. Section 2-201(2) applies only to a confirmation that is "sufficient against the sender" under subsection (1): a signed writing that indicates a contract for sale has been made and states a quantity. See Problem 2-10(a).
topic: Tier 3 · Statute of frauds (§ 2-201) — Confirmation not sufficient against the sender

q: A contract for a commercial espresso machine says, conspicuously: "SELLER'S SOLE OBLIGATION FOR DEFECTIVE GOODS IS TO REPAIR OR REPLACE THEM." It doesn't mention merchantability. The machine is defective. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The merchantability warranty still exists; the clause only limits the remedy for breaching it.
The clause is void, because a clause dealing with defects must mention merchantability.
The buyer may ignore the clause, because a limited remedy must use the word "exclusive."
The clause disclaims merchantability, because it describes the seller's only obligation.
The clause is effective only if the buyer signed it separately from the rest of the contract.
oe: Correct. A disclaimer narrows what the seller promises (§ 2-316). A remedy limitation leaves the warranty intact and restricts what the buyer recovers when it's breached (§§ 2-316(4), 2-719). This clause is a remedy limitation.
The mention requirement applies to disclaimers, not to remedy limitations.
The clause says "sole obligation," which signals an exclusive remedy (§ 2-719(1)(b)).
The clause doesn't mention merchantability and doesn't say there is no warranty. It limits the remedy.
Neither § 2-316 nor § 2-719 requires a separate signature.
topic: Tier 1 · Warranty disclaimers (§ 2-316) — Remedy limitation is not a disclaimer

q: Big Bird signs a written contract to buy a delivery van. The writing is complete on its face and contains a merger clause. Big Bird offers evidence that, at signing, both parties orally agreed the contract wouldn't take effect unless his bank approved financing, which it didn't. Is the evidence admissible?
o: Yes, but only if the written contract is ambiguous about whether financing was required.
No, because a condition must be in writing to be enforceable under the statute of frauds.
No, because a financing condition contradicts the writing's unconditional promise to buy.
Yes, because the rule doesn't bar proof of an oral condition to the contract taking effect.
No, because the merger clause bars evidence of any contemporaneous oral agreement.
oe: Ambiguity isn't required for evidence that falls outside the rule.
The statute of frauds concerns whether a contract is enforceable, not proof of a condition.
Courts treat a condition to effectiveness as outside the rule rather than as a contradictory term.
Correct. The rule applies only to evidence offered to add or vary terms of an agreement. Evidence that the writing never became effective, such as a condition precedent, is outside it.
The merger clause bars terms of an effective agreement, not proof that no agreement took effect.
topic: Tier 2 · Parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) — Condition precedent to effectiveness

q: After a seller properly demands assurance in writing, the buyer promptly sends audited financial statements and a letter from its bank confirming a healthy credit line. The seller insists on an irrevocable letter of credit for the full contract amount and keeps suspending shipments when the buyer won't provide one. What is the most likely result?
o: The seller is likely in breach, because the buyer's assurance was adequate.
The seller is protected, because a letter of credit is the only acceptable assurance of payment.
The buyer is in breach, because it refused to provide the letter of credit that was demanded.
Neither party is in breach, because the contract is suspended until they agree.
The seller is protected, because the party demanding assurance decides what is adequate.
oe: Correct. What counts as adequate assurance is judged by commercial standards (§ 2-609(2)). Once adequate assurance is given, the right to suspend ends. Demanding more than is adequate and continuing to withhold performance can itself be a repudiation. See Problem 6-3(b).
Many forms of assurance can be adequate, including proof of solvency and available credit.
Refusing an excessive demand isn't a repudiation once adequate assurance has been given.
Suspension lasts only until adequate assurance is received.
Adequacy is an objective commercial question, not the demanding party's choice.
topic: Tier 2 · Insecurity & repudiation (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Adequate assurance given; seller over-demands

q: Sweetums sells a used food truck to Floyd. Before signing, Floyd learns that a bank holds a recorded security interest in the truck, and he buys anyway at a discount. The bank later repossesses the truck when Sweetums defaults on the loan. Floyd sues Sweetums for breach of the warranty of title. What is the most likely result?
o: Sweetums wins, because a security interest has nothing to do with the warranty of title.
Sweetums wins, because Floyd knew of the security interest when he contracted.
Floyd wins, because an unpaid security interest makes title defective whatever the buyer knew.
Floyd wins, because every seller warrants that its goods are free of all liens.
Floyd wins, but only if the bank's security interest had not been publicly recorded.
oe: Freedom from undisclosed security interests is part of the title warranty.
Correct. The seller warrants that the goods will be delivered free from any security interest or lien "of which the buyer at the time of contracting has no knowledge" (§ 2-312(1)(b)). Floyd knew.
Section 2-312(1)(b) turns on the buyer's knowledge.
The warranty excludes liens the buyer knew of when contracting.
Recording doesn't decide it. Floyd's actual knowledge does.
topic: Tier 1 · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-403) — Known security interest

q: An optometrist examines Ernie's eyes, prescribes contact lenses, and sells him a supply of them. The lenses are defectively made and irritate his eyes. In a jurisdiction that applies the gravamen-of-the-action test to mixed goods-and-services transactions, does Article 2 govern Ernie's claim?
o: No, because the predominant purpose of an optometrist's visit is professional services.
No, because medical professionals are never merchants.
Yes, because every transaction involving goods is governed entirely by Article 2.
Yes, because the claim arises from the defective lenses, which are goods.
No, because the lenses were incidental to the exam.
oe: That's the predominant-purpose test, which looks at the whole transaction. The gravamen test looks at the claim.
Whether Article 2 applies doesn't turn on merchant status.
Mixed transactions need a test, and under the gravamen test, claims about the services may fall outside Article 2.

Correct. The gravamen test asks whether the claim concerns the goods or the services in a mixed transaction. A claim about defective lenses is about the goods, so Article 2 applies to it, even if a claim about the eye exam would not be governed by Article 2.
Under the gravamen test, how much of the deal the goods made up doesn't matter if the claim is about them.
topic: Tier 3 · Scope, goods & merchants (§§ 2-102, 2-105, 2-107) — Gravamen test

q: A thief steals Prairie Dawn's bicycle and sells it to Crazy Harry's Cycles, a used-bike shop that buys in good faith. Crazy Harry's sells it to Herry, a good-faith buyer in the ordinary course of business. Prairie Dawn finds it and sues Herry to recover it. Who wins?
o: Herry, because two good-faith purchases in a row cut off the original owner's rights.
Herry, because Crazy Harry's bought in good faith for value and so had voidable title.
Herry, because he bought in the ordinary course from a merchant that deals in bicycles.
Prairie Dawn, because a thief gets void title, and she entrusted the bike to no one.
None of the above.
oe: The number of good-faith transfers doesn't cure a void title.
A good-faith purchaser from a thief gets nothing, so Crazy Harry's had no title to pass.
Being a buyer in ordinary course helps only under the entrustment rule, which doesn't apply to stolen goods.

Correct. A purchaser takes only the title its transferor had or had power to transfer (§ 2-403(1)). A thief has void title. The entrustment rule in § 2-403(2) protects buyers only when the owner entrusted the goods to the merchant, and Prairie Dawn didn't.
One of the other choices is correct: Prairie Dawn, because a thief gets void title, and she entrusted the bike to no one.
topic: Tier 1 · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-403) — Thief; then merchant; then ordinary-course buyer

q: A contract calls for 12 monthly deliveries of 1,000 printed labels. In the fourth delivery, 50 labels are misprinted. The defect doesn't substantially impair the value of the whole contract, and the seller promptly offers to replace them within a week and assures the buyer it will. The buyer wants to reject the entire fourth delivery. May it?
o: Yes, because under the perfect tender rule a buyer may reject any delivery that fails to conform in any respect.
No, because the defect can be cured and the seller has given adequate assurance that it will cure.
No, because a buyer under an installment contract must accept every delivery and sue for damages instead.
Yes, and because one installment was defective, the buyer may also cancel the rest of the contract.
Yes, but only if the buyer is a consumer, because merchants must accept installments that can be cured.
oe: Section 2-601 is expressly subject to § 2-612 for installment contracts.
Correct. Section 2-612(2) replaces perfect tender for installments. If the nonconformity can be cured and the seller gives adequate assurance of cure, the buyer must accept the installment.
A buyer may reject an installment that is substantially impaired and can't be cured.
Cancellation of the whole requires a nonconformity that substantially impairs the value of the whole contract (§ 2-612(3)).
Section 2-612 applies regardless of the parties' status.
topic: Tier 2 · Tender, inspection, acceptance & payment — Installment contract; curable defect

q: Before selling a used air compressor to Kermit, Gonzo's Equipment Rental says, in a recorded phone call, "Understand that we're not giving you any warranty of merchantability on this compressor." Kermit says, "Fine." Nothing about warranties appears in writing. The compressor fails in ordinary use. Was the merchantability warranty effectively disclaimed?
o: No, because every warranty disclaimer must be in writing.
Yes, but only because Kermit is a merchant.
No, because a disclaimer must use the words "as is" or "with all faults."
No, because an oral disclaimer can't be conspicuous.
None of the above.
oe: Only a fitness disclaimer must be in writing. A merchantability disclaimer can be oral.
The rule is the same for consumers. Merchant status doesn't change § 2-316(2).
That's one alternative under § 2-316(3)(a). Mentioning merchantability under § 2-316(2) is another.
Conspicuousness applies only to a written disclaimer.

Correct. The disclaimer was effective, but none of the reasons given is right. Under § 2-316(2), language excluding merchantability "must mention merchantability and in case of a writing must be conspicuous." An oral disclaimer that mentions merchantability works, whether the buyer is a merchant or a consumer.
topic: Tier 1 · Warranty disclaimers (§ 2-316) — Oral disclaimer of merchantability

q: A signed contract for 100 steel beams at $20,000 says: "Seller may not assign this contract." Seller then assigns its right to the $20,000 payment to Sesame Bank, and the bank notifies the buyer. The buyer argues the assignment is ineffective. What is the most likely result?
o: Effective, but it also delegates the seller's duty to deliver the beams to the bank.
Ineffective, because assigning the payment materially increases the buyer's burden.
Effective, because a ban on assigning "the contract" is read to bar only delegating the seller's duties.
Effective only if the buyer consents in writing to the assignment of the payment.
Ineffective, because the contract expressly prohibits the seller from assigning it.
oe: The seller assigned only the right to payment. It didn't assign the contract generally.
Assigning a right to payment normally doesn't change the buyer's duty at all.

Correct. "Unless the circumstances indicate the contrary, a prohibition of assignment of 'the contract' is to be construed as barring only the delegation to the assignee of the assignor's performance" (§ 2-210(4)). Assigning the right to payment is outside it.
An assignment of rights doesn't need the other party's consent.
Section 2-210(4) reads the clause narrowly, as a bar on delegation only.
topic: Tier 2 · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210) — "May not assign this contract" bars only delegation

q: A contract for 500 bales of cotton says the price "will be set by an independent appraiser chosen by Buyer." After the seller delivers, the buyer refuses to choose an appraiser. Which statement is most accurate?
o: There's no contract, because the price was never fixed by the appraiser.
The seller may treat the contract as canceled or fix a reasonable price.
The seller must sue to force the buyer to choose an appraiser before it can be paid.
The buyer may set any price it chooses, because it controlled the choice of appraiser.
The price is the market price for cotton on the date the contract was made.
oe: Section 2-305(3) gives the innocent party options precisely because the failure was the other party's fault.

Correct. "When a price left to be fixed otherwise than by agreement of the parties fails to be fixed through fault of one party the other may at his option treat the contract as cancelled or himself fix a reasonable price" (§ 2-305(3)). See Problem 4-3(c).
Article 2 gives the seller self-help options instead.
The buyer is the party at fault and gets no such power.
Nothing in § 2-305 uses the date of contracting.
topic: Tier 2 · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Price fixed by the buyer; buyer won't act

q: Two college roommates, neither of whom is a merchant, agree on a $600 sale of a used electric guitar. Does Article 2 govern the sale?
o: No, because Article 2 applies only when at least one of the parties is a merchant.
No, because the common law of contracts governs sales between two consumers.
Yes, because Article 2 covers sales of goods whether or not a merchant is involved.
No, because used goods sold between individuals aren't covered by Article 2.
Yes, but only because the price is $500 or more, which brings it within Article 2.
oe: Merchant status triggers particular rules, such as § 2-314, not the Article's coverage.
The common law supplements Article 2 (§ 1-103(b)) but doesn't displace it.
Correct. Article 2 applies to "transactions in goods" (§ 2-102). Some provisions apply only to merchants, but the Article governs all sales of goods. See Problem 1-4.
Used goods are goods.
The $500 threshold affects the statute of frauds, not coverage.
topic: Tier 3 · Scope, goods & merchants (§§ 2-102, 2-105, 2-107) — Consumer-to-consumer sale

q: Before the first of three installments is due, a manufacturer writes to the buyer: "Your design drawings were incomplete. We have revised them, but we must retool, which will add expense and some delay. We will not be able to deliver the first installment on time. We expect you to cover the extra expense. We anticipate catching up by the second installment." Which statement is most accurate?
o: It is a valid modification of the contract that the buyer must accept.
It is a repudiation, because the manufacturer says it won't deliver the first installment on time.
It is a repudiation, because the manufacturer demands that the buyer pay the extra expense.
Probably not a repudiation, but it likely gives the buyer reasonable grounds for insecurity.
It has no legal effect, because only a formal written notice can be a repudiation.
oe: A modification requires agreement. A one-sided letter isn't one.
Announcing a delay while promising to catch up isn't a clear refusal to perform the contract, though it may breach the first installment when it comes due.
An expectation of reimbursement isn't a repudiation unless performance is conditioned on it.

Correct. A repudiation requires a clear statement or action showing a party won't perform. A mere request for a change in terms isn't one unless performance is conditioned on it (§ 2-610 cmt. 2). The letter expects reimbursement but doesn't refuse to perform without it, and its warning of delay justifies a demand for assurance under § 2-609. See Problem 6-5.
Repudiation can occur by words or conduct, and the letter at least supports insecurity.
topic: Tier 2 · Insecurity & repudiation (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Is this letter a repudiation?

q: In January, Farmer Gonzo signs a contract to sell Camilla all the sweet corn that will be grown that summer on his north field. He plants the field in May, and the corn is harvested in August. When were the goods identified to the contract?
o: When the corn is shipped or marked for Camilla.
In May, when the corn was planted and became a growing crop.
In August, when the corn was harvested.
In January, when the contract was made.
Never, because growing crops aren't goods until they're severed from the land.
oe: That's the rule for other future goods under § 2-501(1)(b). Crops have their own rule.
Correct. For crops to be harvested within twelve months or the next normal harvest season, identification occurs "when the crops are planted or otherwise become growing crops" (§ 2-501(1)(c)).
Harvest isn't the trigger under § 2-501(1)(c). Planting is.
Identification at contracting applies to goods that are already existing and identified. The corn didn't exist yet.
Growing crops are goods (§§ 2-105(1), 2-107(2)).
topic: Tier 1 · Risk of loss & identification (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510) — Identification of crops

q: Fozzie tells a hardware-store clerk, "I need a ladder to clean the gutters on my two-story house." The clerk recommends a 24-foot extension ladder, and Fozzie buys it. The first time he uses it on his gutters, set up properly, a rung splits under his ordinary weight. Which warranty claim fits best?
o: Both, because Fozzie relied on the clerk's recommendation in choosing the ladder.
Neither, because the clerk only recommended the ladder and Fozzie decided to buy it.
Fitness for a particular purpose, because Fozzie told the clerk exactly how he would use it.
Express warranty, because the clerk's recommendation was an affirmation of fact about it.
Merchantability, because reaching gutters is an ordinary use of an extension ladder.
oe: Reliance matters only if there is a particular purpose. Here the use is ordinary.
Merchantability doesn't depend on reliance, and the store is a merchant that deals in ladders.
Telling the seller about an ordinary use doesn't turn it into a particular purpose.
A bare recommendation isn't an affirmation of fact about the ladder.

Correct. A particular purpose is a specific use peculiar to the buyer, different from the goods' ordinary use (§ 2-315 cmt. 2). Climbing an extension ladder to reach gutters is what such ladders are for, so the claim lies under § 2-314(2)(c).
topic: Tier 1 · Implied warranties (§§ 2-314, 2-315) — Ordinary vs. particular purpose

q: Boober buys a hand loom from Mokey, a weaver selling her spare equipment, for $1,800. He pays with a check and takes the loom home. The check bounces. Before Mokey can act, Boober sells the loom for $1,600 to Wembley, who knows nothing of the problem. Mokey sues Wembley to recover the loom. Who wins?
o: Wembley, but only if Boober is a merchant who regularly deals in looms.
Mokey, because a buyer who pays with a bad check gets no title at all to pass on.
Mokey, because Wembley paid $200 less than the price Boober had agreed to pay.
Wembley, because Boober had voidable title and Wembley bought in good faith for value.
None of the above.
oe: Voidable-title protection under § 2-403(1) doesn't depend on the transferor being a merchant. That's the entrustment rule.
A bad check gives the buyer voidable title, not void title.
Value doesn't have to equal the original price. Paying $1,600 is value.

Correct. A person with voidable title has power to transfer good title to a good-faith purchaser for value, even when the goods were delivered in exchange for a check that was later dishonored (§ 2-403(1)(b)). Mokey's remedy is against Boober.
One of the other choices is correct: Wembley, because Boober had voidable title and Wembley bought in good faith for value.
topic: Tier 1 · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-403) — Voidable title from a bounced check

q: A seller contracts to supply corrugated boxes at a fixed price. Months later, a mill fire across the region causes the price of the seller's raw paperboard to triple, so continuing at the contract price would cause heavy losses. The seller explains the situation and asks for a 15% increase, and the buyer agrees in an email. Later, the buyer refuses to pay the increase, arguing it got nothing new in return. What is the most likely result?
o: The seller wins only if the modification was in a writing signed by both of the parties.
The buyer wins, because the seller was already legally obligated to perform at the original price.
The buyer wins, because the cost increase would have excused the seller under § 2-615 anyway.
The buyer wins, because the seller gave no new consideration for the 15% increase.
The seller wins, because a good-faith modification is binding without consideration.
oe: Unless the contract has a no-oral-modification clause or the modified deal falls within § 2-201, no particular writing is required. An email from the buyer would likely satisfy either anyway.
That is the common-law pre-existing duty rule, which § 2-209(1) displaces.
A cost increase alone usually doesn't excuse performance under § 2-615, but that doesn't matter when the parties agreed to modify.
Article 2 doesn't require consideration for a modification.

Correct. Section 2-209(1) makes modifications binding without consideration. An unforeseen market shift that makes performance unexpectedly burdensome is a legitimate commercial reason for seeking one in good faith (§ 2-209 cmt. 2).
topic: Tier 2 · Modification (§ 2-209) — Good-faith modification after an unforeseen cost rise

q: A music store's invoice to Floyd describes a guitar as "1959 Gibson Les Paul Standard, original finish." The store honestly believed that was true. A year later, an appraiser shows it's a 1974 reissue. The store argues it made no warranty because (1) it never used the word "warrant" or "guarantee," and (2) it honestly believed the description. Which statement is correct?
o: Neither works, because a description that is part of the bargain is a warranty either way.
Neither works, but Floyd must still prove that he relied on the invoice in deciding to buy.
Both arguments work, so Floyd's only remedy is a claim for fraud or misrepresentation.
Argument (2) works, because an honest mistake about the goods isn't a breach of warranty.
Argument (1) works, because express warranties require formal words such as "warrant."
oe: Correct. A description of the goods creates an express warranty that the goods will conform (§ 2-313(1)(b)). No formal words like "warrant" or "guarantee" are needed, and the seller need not intend to make a warranty (§ 2-313(2)). Warranty liability doesn't depend on fault.
Comment 3 to § 2-313 says no particular reliance need be shown for affirmations made during the bargain.
Neither argument works, and Floyd doesn't have to prove fraud.
Warranty is strict liability. The seller's good faith is irrelevant.
Section 2-313(2) says the opposite: no formal words are necessary.
topic: Tier 1 · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Description; seller's good faith

q: Gobo agrees to sell 40 pallets of radish seed to Wembley. The contract says: "Seller will ship the goods to Buyer's warehouse, 12 Rock Road, Fraggleton." It has no F.O.B. or other delivery term. Gobo delivers the seed to a reputable carrier, makes a reasonable shipping contract, and emails Wembley the tracking details. The truck overturns and the seed is ruined. Must Wembley pay?
o: Yes, but only if Wembley had already paid for the seed before it shipped.
Yes, because risk passed when Gobo duly delivered the seed to the carrier.
No, because naming the buyer's warehouse in the contract makes it a destination contract.
No, because the carrier, not the buyer, is responsible for losses during transit.
No, because Wembley never received the seed, and risk passes only on the buyer's receipt.
oe: Payment has nothing to do with when risk passes.

Correct. Article 2 presumes a shipment contract. A "ship to" instruction only names where the goods are going; it doesn't make the seller responsible for delivering them there (§ 2-503 cmt. 5). Gobo met its § 2-504 duties, so risk passed under § 2-509(1)(a).
Naming the buyer's address doesn't create a destination contract. The seller must expressly agree to deliver at a particular destination, as with "F.O.B. buyer's warehouse."
The carrier may be liable to whoever bears the risk, but between seller and buyer the risk had passed to Wembley.
Receipt is the rule for a merchant seller in a non-shipment case under § 2-509(3). Here the goods were shipped by carrier, so § 2-509(1) applies.
topic: Tier 1 · Risk of loss & identification (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510) — "Ship to" term is a shipment contract

q: A gallery agrees to sell a specific etching to a collector, with payment due on delivery the next day. That evening, the etching's true owner, from whom it had been stolen years earlier, recovers it from the gallery by court order. The gallery argues the contract is avoided as a casualty to identified goods. What is the most likely result?
o: The gallery isn't excused, because it never had good title and so breached the title warranty.
The contract is avoided under § 2-615, because performance became impossible for the gallery.
The collector must pay, because the etching was identified to the contract when it was made.
The contract is avoided, because the loss happened before risk passed and without the gallery's fault.
The gallery is excused if it acted in good faith and didn't know the etching was stolen.
oe: Correct. Section 2-613 covers casualty such as fire, flood, or theft, without fault of either party. A seller that never had good title can't pass it, and the reclamation reveals a breach of the § 2-312 warranty. See Problem 6-6(b).
The impossibility comes from the seller's own lack of title, which is a risk the seller bears.
The collector never received the etching, and the gallery couldn't deliver good title.
Recovery by the true owner exposes the seller's own title defect. It isn't a fortuitous casualty.
Good faith isn't a defense to breach of the title warranty.
topic: Tier 2 · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-615) — Goods reclaimed by their owner isn't a casualty

q: Courts weigh freedom of contract against protecting weaker parties when they review warranty disclaimers. In which transaction are courts most likely to scrutinize a disclaimer closely?
o: A sale of new, prepackaged consumer goods to an individual.
A negotiated sale of commercial goods between merchants with lawyers.
Courts apply the same level of scrutiny to every transaction.
A sale of specially made commercial equipment between two merchants.
A sale of used goods between two merchants.
oe: Correct. On the continuum from freedom of contract to protection, new consumer goods sit at the protective end: the buyer can't negotiate, can't inspect what's inside, and expects the goods to work.
Sophisticated, represented parties get the least protection.
Courts apply § 2-316 to all sales, but how closely they review issues like conspicuousness and surprise varies with the buyer's need for protection.
Negotiated merchant deals for custom goods sit at the freedom-of-contract end.
Used goods and merchant parties both point toward freedom of contract.
topic: Tier 1 · Warranty disclaimers (§ 2-316) — The protection continuum

q: A theater orally orders 300 custom seats embroidered with its logo from Sweetums Seating for $45,000. Before Sweetums orders any materials or begins any work, the theater calls to cancel. Sweetums sues, and the theater raises the statute of frauds. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Sweetums wins, because seats embroidered with the logo aren't suitable for sale to others.
Sweetums wins, but only for the portion of the seats it could have made before trial.
The theater wins, because Sweetums hadn't begun work before the theater canceled.
The theater wins, because oral contracts for goods are never enforceable.
Sweetums wins, because the exception applies whenever the buyer orders custom-made goods.
oe: That's one element. The seller also needs a substantial beginning before notice of repudiation.
No portion is enforceable when the exception's timing element isn't met.

Correct. Section 2-201(3)(a) applies only if the seller, "before notice of repudiation is received and under circumstances which reasonably indicate that the goods are for the buyer, has made either a substantial beginning of their manufacture or commitments for their procurement."
Oral contracts can be enforced under the § 2-201(3) exceptions.
The exception has several elements, including timing.
topic: Tier 3 · Statute of frauds (§ 2-201) — Specially manufactured goods: timing of repudiation

q: A farmer agrees to sell 100 bushels of wheat to a miller. The contract doesn't say where delivery will occur. When it's made, the wheat is in the farmer's barn on the farm where he does business. Later, the farmer moves the wheat to a storage site 300 miles away and calls the miller: "Your wheat is ready. Pick it up at the storage site." Has the farmer made a proper tender?
o: No, because when the contract is silent the seller must deliver the goods to the buyer's mill.
Yes, because the seller is free to choose where to tender delivery when the contract is silent.
Yes, because the wheat was identified to the contract, so it could be tendered wherever it sat.
No, because absent agreement the place for delivery is the seller's place of business.
Yes, because the farmer told the miller exactly where the wheat was and that it was ready.
oe: Absent agreement, Article 2 doesn't require delivery at the buyer's place.
The manner, time, and place of tender are set by the agreement and Article 2 (§ 2-503(1)), not by the seller alone.
Identification doesn't change the place for delivery.

Correct. The place for delivery is the seller's place of business (§ 2-308(a)), unless the contract is for identified goods known by both parties when contracting to be elsewhere (§ 2-308(b)). The storage site wasn't known when they contracted. See Problem 4-4(a)(4).
Notice is necessary but doesn't make an improper place proper.
topic: Tier 2 · Tender, inspection, acceptance & payment — Tender at a different place

q: Uncle Traveling Matt orally agrees to buy 100 hiking packs from Cantus's Outfitters for $6,000. He pays $2,400 for 40 packs, and Cantus's accepts the payment. Cantus's then refuses to deliver any packs, and Matt sues. There's no writing, and Cantus's denies the deal in its pleadings. To what extent is the contract enforceable?
o: Not at all, because there's no writing.
Only as to the 40 packs that were paid for.
As to all 100 packs, because part performance takes the whole contract out of the statute.
As to all 100, because Cantus's accepted payment.
None of the above.
oe: Section 2-201(3)(c) makes the paid-for portion enforceable.

Correct. A contract that doesn't satisfy § 2-201(1) is enforceable "with respect to goods for which payment has been made and accepted or which have been received and accepted" (§ 2-201(3)(c)). The exception doesn't reach the other 60.
Article 2's part-performance exception is limited to the goods paid for or received.
Acceptance of payment validates only the goods covered by that payment.
One of the other choices is correct: Only as to the 40 packs that were paid for.
topic: Tier 3 · Statute of frauds (§ 2-201) — Part performance: only to the extent paid

q: A coin collector agrees to buy a rare 1909-S VDB penny from a dealer for $2,000. Is the penny "goods" under Article 2?
o: No, because money is excluded from the definition of goods in every case.
No, because rare coins bought as collectibles are investment securities.
Yes, because money sold as a commodity, rather than used to pay, is goods.
Yes, but only because the price exceeds the coin's face value by more than $500.
No, because a coin is a thing in action, which § 2-105 excludes.
oe: Only money used to pay the price is excluded.
Investment securities are Article 8 interests such as stock, not physical collectibles.
Correct. Section 2-105(1) excludes only "the money in which the price is to be paid." Comment 1 explains that money treated as a commodity, such as a rare coin, is goods. See Problem 1-1(B).
The amount of the markup doesn't determine whether it's goods.
A thing in action is a right to sue, such as a debt. A physical coin isn't one.
topic: Tier 3 · Scope, goods & merchants (§§ 2-102, 2-105, 2-107) — Money as goods

q: A franchise agreement lets an oil company set the price at which it sells gasoline to its franchised stations. The company sets a price within the range its competitors charge, but evidence shows it chose the price as part of a plan to squeeze franchisees out of business and replace them with company-run stations. Under Mathis v. Exxon, which statement is most accurate?
o: It is in good faith unless the franchisees prove the price was higher than the prevailing market price.
It is unenforceable, because Article 2 never lets one party fix the price under a contract for sale.
It is necessarily in good faith, because a price within the range competitors charge is commercially reasonable.
Under Mathis, it can still breach good faith, though many courts treat a market-range posted price as safe.
It can be reviewed only for unconscionability, because good faith doesn't apply to price terms.
oe: Under Mathis, subjective bad faith can be shown even with a market-range price.
Section 2-305(2) expressly permits a price to be fixed by one party.
That's the safe-harbor view many courts take, but it isn't what Mathis held.

Correct. A price to be fixed by the seller must be fixed in good faith (§ 2-305(2)). Mathis held that a commercially reasonable price can still be set in bad faith if the seller's subjective purpose is dishonest. Other courts read comment 3 as making a posted price within the market range a safe harbor.
Section 2-305(2) imposes a good-faith standard.
topic: Tier 2 · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Price set by the seller; good faith

q: Under § 1-201(b)(10), which of the following would NOT ordinarily make a disclaimer conspicuous?
o: Body text set off from the surrounding text by symbols or other marks that call attention to it.
A heading in capital letters in a larger type than the surrounding text of the same or lesser size.
Placing it just above the signature line, in the same type as everything else.
Body text in a contrasting color from the surrounding text.
Body text in larger type than the surrounding text.
oe: This is a statutory example (§ 1-201(b)(10)(B)).
This is a statutory example (§ 1-201(b)(10)(A)).
Correct. Location near the signature, without any difference in type or other attention-getting feature, isn't one of the statute's examples, and a reasonable person might not notice it.
This is a statutory example (§ 1-201(b)(10)(B)).
This is a statutory example (§ 1-201(b)(10)(B)).
topic: Tier 1 · Warranty disclaimers (§ 2-316) — Conspicuous: which does NOT qualify

q: A hotel contracts with a celebrated glass artist, Camilla, to create and sell it a one-of-a-kind chandelier designed and made by Camilla herself. Short on time, Camilla delegates the job to a skilled apprentice. The hotel objects. May Camilla delegate?
o: No, because any delegation of a duty requires the other party's consent.
No, because the hotel has a substantial interest in Camilla's own performance.
Yes, because both buyers and sellers are generally free to delegate their duties.
Yes, because the contract between Camilla and the hotel doesn't prohibit delegation.
Yes, as long as Camilla remains liable to the hotel if the apprentice's work is defective.
oe: Delegation generally needs no consent. The bar here comes from the hotel's substantial interest.

Correct. A party may perform through a delegate "unless otherwise agreed or unless the other party has a substantial interest in having his original promisor perform or control the acts required by the contract" (§ 2-210(1)). A commission for an artist's own work is the classic example.
That's the general rule, but it gives way when the other party has a substantial interest in the original promisor's performance.
Even without a prohibition, delegation is barred when the other party has a substantial interest in the original performance.
Continued liability is the consequence of a permitted delegation. It doesn't make this delegation permissible.
topic: Tier 2 · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210) — Substantial interest in personal performance

q: Statler sells 200 theater seats to Waldorf, "F.O.B. Statler's factory." Statler properly packs the seats, hands them to a carrier, and makes a reasonable shipping contract, but forgets to tell Waldorf the seats have shipped. An hour into the trip, the carrier's truck catches fire and the seats are destroyed. Waldorf argues he bears no risk because Statler never notified him. Who is right?
o: Statler, because missing notice matters only if it causes material delay or loss.
Statler, but only because both parties are merchants in the theater-seat business.
Waldorf, because under F.O.B. seller's factory, risk passes only when the buyer is notified.
Neither, because the loss is split when both parties were partly responsible.
Waldorf, because a seller that skips any of its shipping duties keeps the risk of loss.
oe: Correct. Prompt notice is one of the seller's shipping duties under § 2-504(c), but the last sentence of § 2-504 makes failure to notify a ground for rejection only if material delay or loss ensues. The fire had nothing to do with the missing notice, so risk passed under § 2-509(1)(a).
Merchant status matters under § 2-509(3), not in shipment contracts. The result would be the same for non-merchants.
Under F.O.B. place of shipment, the seller bears risk only until the goods are in the carrier's possession (§ 2-319(1)(a)). Notice isn't the trigger.
Neither party caused the fire, and Article 2 has no comparative-fault allocation of risk.
The UCC deliberately limits the effect of a notice failure to cases where it causes material delay or loss.
topic: Tier 1 · Risk of loss & identification (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510) — Seller fails to notify; loss not caused by it

q: A con artist tells Sweetums, a private seller, that he is the famous composer Rowlf and buys Sweetums's piano, paying with a forged cashier's check. He sells the piano the next day to Janice, who pays fair value in good faith. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Janice gets good title only if Sweetums, the original seller, was a merchant.
Janice gets good title only if she bought from a merchant who deals in pianos.
Sweetums keeps title, because a sale obtained by impersonating someone else is void from the start.
Janice gets good title, because deceit about identity gives voidable title, not void title.
Sweetums keeps title, because paying with a forged check is a crime, and criminals get no title.
oe: The seller's merchant status is irrelevant to § 2-403(1).
That's the entrustment rule. Section 2-403(1) protects good-faith purchasers from any holder of voidable title.
Section 2-403(1)(a) treats deception about identity as producing voidable, not void, title.

Correct. When goods are delivered under a transaction of purchase, the purchaser can transfer good title to a good-faith purchaser for value even though "the transferor was deceived as to the identity of the purchaser" (§ 2-403(1)(a)).
Even delivery "procured through fraud punishable as larcenous under the criminal law" gives voidable title (§ 2-403(1)(d)).
topic: Tier 1 · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-403) — Impostor

q: A grocery chain rightfully rejects a delivery of 500 pounds of strawberries that arrived moldy in part. The seller has no agent or place of business in the buyer's city, and it doesn't respond to the buyer's request for instructions. The berries that are still good will spoil within a day or two. What must the buyer do?
o: Destroy the strawberries, because the seller abandoned them.
Hold the strawberries until the seller picks them up, even if they spoil.
Use the good strawberries in its own stores, which is consistent with the rejection.
Nothing, because once goods are rightfully rejected the buyer has no further obligations.
Make reasonable efforts to sell the strawberries for the seller's account.
oe: The buyer must try to salvage their value by resale.
For perishables with no instructions, a merchant buyer must try to resell them.
Using the goods as its own would be an act inconsistent with the seller's ownership and could be an acceptance.
A merchant buyer has the extra duties in § 2-603 for perishable goods.

Correct. A merchant buyer that has rightfully rejected goods in its possession, when the seller has no agent or place of business at the market of rejection, must follow the seller's reasonable instructions, and without them must make reasonable efforts to sell perishable goods for the seller's account (§ 2-603(1)).
topic: Tier 2 · Tender, inspection, acceptance & payment — Merchant buyer's duty for perishables

q: Kermit and Fozzie orally agree that Kermit will sell Fozzie 100 rubber chickens for $400. Before any performance, they orally agree to double both the quantity and the price, to 200 chickens for $800. Nothing is in writing. Which statement is most accurate?
o: It is enforceable for all 200 chickens, because both parties agreed to the change.
It is enforceable, because a modification needs no consideration to be binding.
Neither the original agreement nor the modified one is enforceable.
It isn't enforceable without a record, because the modified contract is for $800.
It is enforceable, because the original contract was for less than $500 and needed no writing.
oe: Without a record, § 2-201 bars enforcement of the $800 contract as modified.
Consideration isn't the issue. Section 2-209(3) brings in the statute of frauds.
The original $400 agreement needed no writing. At most, the parties are left with it, subject to any waiver or reliance argument.

Correct. "The requirements of the statute of frauds section of this Article must be satisfied if the contract as modified is within its provisions" (§ 2-209(3)). The modified $800 contract needs a record. See Problem 3-4(a).
What matters is the contract as modified.
topic: Tier 2 · Modification (§ 2-209) — Modification raises the price over $500

q: Which of the following is a consequence of identifying goods to a contract under § 2-501?
o: The risk of loss passes from the seller to the buyer.
Title to the goods passes from the seller to the buyer.
The buyer gets a special property and an insurable interest.
The buyer must pay the price immediately, before delivery.
The seller loses its insurable interest in the goods.
oe: Risk passes under §§ 2-509 and 2-510, which don't turn on identification.
Title passes under § 2-401, usually when the seller completes physical delivery, unless otherwise agreed.
Correct. Identification gives the buyer a special property and an insurable interest (§ 2-501(1)). It's also a prerequisite for some remedies, such as replevin and § 2-613 excuse.
Payment is due when and where the buyer is to receive the goods unless otherwise agreed (§ 2-310(a)). Identification doesn't accelerate payment.
The seller keeps an insurable interest as long as it has title or a security interest (§ 2-501(2)).
topic: Tier 1 · Risk of loss & identification (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510) — Effect of identification

q: On the back of a four-page purchase agreement for an industrial dishwasher, paragraph 19 of 31 reads: "Seller disclaims the implied warranty of merchantability." It's printed in the same small, plain type as every other paragraph, with no heading. The buyer never read it. The dishwasher fails in ordinary use. Is merchantability effectively disclaimed?
o: No, because a written disclaimer of merchantability must be conspicuous, and this one isn't.
Yes, because the buyer signed the agreement and is bound by everything in it.
Yes, because the clause expressly mentions merchantability, as § 2-316(2) requires.
Yes, because both parties are businesses and should read their contracts.
No, because merchantability can never be disclaimed in a sale of new goods.
oe: Correct. A term is conspicuous if a reasonable person ought to have noticed it, for example through a heading in capitals or larger, contrasting type (§ 1-201(b)(10)). A clause buried in identical small print isn't conspicuous, so § 2-316(2) isn't satisfied.
Signing doesn't cure the lack of conspicuousness that § 2-316(2) requires.
Mentioning merchantability is necessary, but a written disclaimer must also be conspicuous.
Section 2-316(2) applies between merchants too.
It can be disclaimed by language that meets § 2-316.
topic: Tier 1 · Warranty disclaimers (§ 2-316) — Written disclaimer not conspicuous

q: Before Swedish Chef buys a pizza oven, the seller tells him, "This oven reaches 900 degrees." It reaches only 650. At his deposition, the Chef admits he would probably have bought the oven anyway because the price was so good. The seller argues the statement wasn't part of the basis of the bargain because the Chef didn't rely on it. What is the most likely result under § 2-313 and its comments?
o: The Chef wins only if the seller's statement was made in writing.
The seller wins, because a temperature rating is the seller's opinion, not a fact.
The seller wins, because a buyer who would have bought anyway can't show the statement was part of the bargain.
The Chef wins only if he proves the seller knew the oven couldn't reach 900 degrees.
Probably still a warranty, because the buyer need not prove reliance on the statement.
oe: Oral statements can be express warranties.
A specific, measurable temperature is an affirmation of fact.
That treats basis of the bargain as reliance. Under the comments, the burden is on the seller, and a "probably" admission is unlikely to meet it.
Knowledge of falsity is an element of fraud, not breach of warranty.

Correct. Comment 3 to § 2-313 says no particular reliance need be shown, and that "any fact which is to take such affirmations, once made, out of the agreement requires clear affirmative proof." Saying he would "probably" have bought anyway is weak proof.
topic: Tier 1 · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Basis of the bargain without proof of reliance

q: On March 1, a seller tells a buyer it won't deliver the 5,000 bags of fertilizer due April 1. On March 5, the buyer buys substitute fertilizer from another supplier for the season. On March 8, the seller emails that it has changed its mind and will deliver on April 1 after all. Is the retraction effective?
o: Yes, because the seller retracted before April 1, when its performance was due.
No, because the buyer materially changed its position by covering before the retraction.
Yes, but only if the seller also gives the buyer adequate assurance that it will perform.
No, because once a party repudiates, the repudiation can never be retracted.
Yes, because the buyer never told the seller that it considered the repudiation final.
oe: Timing before the due date isn't enough when the buyer has already changed position.
