Correct. A repudiating party may retract until its next performance is due "unless the aggrieved party has since the repudiation cancelled or materially changed his position or otherwise indicated that he considers the repudiation final" (§ 2-611(1)).
Assurance is required if demanded, but here the retraction comes too late in any event.
Section 2-611 permits retraction in the right circumstances.
Materially changing position, for example by covering, is enough on its own.
topic: Tier 2 · Insecurity & repudiation (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Retraction too late after cover

q: A brewery orders custom fermentation tanks for a new taproom it plans to open on May 1, and tells the seller that time is of the essence. After negotiating, they agree on liquidated damages of $1,500 for each day of inexcusable delay, a figure that fairly estimated the brewery's expected lost profits. The tanks arrive 20 days late. As it turns out, May was unusually slow, and the brewery's actual lost profits were about $5,000. What can the brewery most likely recover?
o: $30,000, because the clause was reasonable in light of the anticipated harm.
Nothing, because Article 2 treats liquidated damages clauses as void penalties.
$5,000, because the liquidated damages clause wasn't printed conspicuously.
$5,000, because liquidated damages can never exceed the buyer's actual damages.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Section 2-718(1) allows liquidated damages "at an amount which is reasonable in the light of the anticipated or actual harm caused by the breach." A clause that was reasonable when made doesn't fail because actual harm turned out lower. See Problem 5-6.
Article 2 enforces reasonable liquidated damages clauses.
Nothing requires a liquidated damages clause to be conspicuous.
The test is reasonableness in light of anticipated or actual harm, not a cap at actual harm.
One of the other choices is correct: $30,000, because the clause was reasonable in light of the anticipated harm.
topic: Tier 2 · Remedies & remedy limits (§§ 2-715, 2-718, 2-719) — Liquidated damages: reasonable in light of anticipated harm

q: Animal buys a new motor scooter from a dealer on May 1 and uses it without trouble for three weeks. On his next ride, the ignition shorts out and the scooter won't start. The dealer argues (1) that the scooter worked for three weeks, so it was merchantable when sold, and (2) that the dealer didn't know of any defect. Which is correct?
o: Argument (1) only.
Argument (2), but only because Animal is a consumer rather than a merchant.
Both arguments are correct.
Argument (2) only.
None of the above.
oe: Three weeks of normal use doesn't prove the scooter was free of defects at sale. A latent defect can appear later.
The buyer's status doesn't make the seller's knowledge relevant.
Neither argument is correct.
The seller's knowledge is irrelevant to an implied warranty claim.

Correct. Neither argument defeats the claim, as long as Animal can show the ignition defect existed when the scooter was sold. A latent defect can surface after weeks of normal use and can be proved circumstantially, and implied warranty liability is strict, so the seller's ignorance is irrelevant. See Problem 3-10(a).
topic: Tier 1 · Implied warranties (§§ 2-314, 2-315) — Defect after weeks of use; seller's knowledge

q: Each of the following appears in a conspicuous written clause in a sale of used restaurant equipment. Which clause, standing alone, most clearly excludes BOTH the implied warranty of merchantability and the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose?
o: "SELLER DISCLAIMS THE IMPLIED WARRANTY OF MERCHANTABILITY."
"THERE ARE NO WARRANTIES WHICH EXTEND BEYOND THE DESCRIPTION ON THE FACE HEREOF."
"BUYER ACCEPTS ALL EQUIPMENT AS IS, WITH ALL FAULTS."
"SELLER DISCLAIMS ANY WARRANTY OF TITLE."
None of the above.
oe: That clause excludes merchantability only. Fitness isn't mentioned or otherwise excluded.
That language is the statute's example for excluding fitness (§ 2-316(2)). It doesn't mention merchantability, so merchantability survives.
Correct. Unless the circumstances indicate otherwise, "as is" and "with all faults" exclude all implied warranties (§ 2-316(3)(a)), even without mentioning merchantability.
That excludes title only (§ 2-312(2)), not the implied warranties of quality.
"As is" excludes both implied warranties.
topic: Tier 1 · Warranty disclaimers (§ 2-316) — Which language excludes both implied warranties

q: A contract for 1,000 bushels of soybeans sets the price at "the closing price on the Chicago board on the delivery date, March 15." On March 15, the exchange is closed all day because of a system failure, so no closing price is set. The parties meant to be bound. What price governs?
o: A reasonable price at the time for delivery.
Whatever price the seller sets in good faith.
There's no contract, because the agreed price mechanism failed.
The next closing price the exchange posts after it reopens, whenever that is.
The last closing price before the contract was signed.
oe: Correct. When the price is to be fixed by an agreed market or other standard set or recorded by a third person and it isn't so set, the price is "a reasonable price at the time for delivery" (§ 2-305(1)(c)). See Problem 4-3(b).
Nothing gave the seller the power to set the price.
Because the parties meant to be bound, § 2-305(1) supplies a reasonable price.
The statute uses a reasonable price at the time for delivery, not a later posted price.
The gap filler looks to the time for delivery, not the time of contracting.
topic: Tier 2 · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Agreed price standard isn't set

q: Gonzo buys a new $30,000 sedan from a dealer. It meets every state and federal safety standard, but a national consumer magazine rates it the lowest in its class for front-impact protection. Gonzo is badly hurt in a high-speed head-on crash and sues for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability. What is the most likely result?
o: Gonzo wins, because serious injuries in a crash show that the car wasn't fit for driving.
The dealer wins, because Gonzo was driving at high speed when the crash happened.
The dealer likely wins, because merchantability doesn't require the safest car in its class.
The dealer wins, because complying with government safety regulations always proves merchantability.
Gonzo wins, because a car rated lowest in its class can't pass without objection in the trade.
oe: Merchantability doesn't promise that a car protects occupants in every crash.
Speed might matter to causation, but the question is whether the car was merchantable. That turns on the minimum standard.

Correct. Merchantability is a minimum standard (§ 2-314(2)). A car that meets all safety regulations and is merely rated lower than its competitors can still pass without objection in the trade and be fit for ordinary driving. See Problem 3-10(d).
Compliance is strong evidence, but it isn't conclusive.
A low comparative rating doesn't by itself make a regulation-compliant car objectionable in the trade.
topic: Tier 1 · Implied warranties (§§ 2-314, 2-315) — Meets regulations but rated low

q: Grover buys a heat pump from a dealer. Nothing was said about a warranty during the sale. When the unit is installed, the box contains an owner's manual stating: "This unit is free from defects in materials and workmanship for one year." Eight months later the compressor fails because of a manufacturing defect. Under the approach of the Official Comments, which statement is most accurate?
o: It can't be a warranty, because Grover gave no consideration in exchange for the promise.
It can be an express warranty, because a post-sale statement can modify the deal without consideration.
It's a warranty only if Grover read the manual before the compressor failed.
It's only an implied warranty, because it appeared in printed materials packed with the goods.
It can't be a warranty, because statements made after the contract is formed are never part of the bargain.
oe: Modifications under § 2-209(1) need no consideration.

Correct. Comment 7 to § 2-313 says the precise time a statement is made isn't controlling, and an affirmation made after the sale can become a modification under § 2-209, which needs no consideration. Some courts disagree, so the answer is "can be." See Problem 3-7.
Under the comment's approach, the statement becomes part of the deal as a modification. Nothing makes reading before failure the test.
A specific promise about freedom from defects is an express affirmation, not an implied term.
Comment 7 rejects a rigid timing rule.
topic: Tier 1 · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Statement made after the sale

q: Uncle Deadly leaves his antique pocket watch with Big Ben's Jewelers for cleaning. Big Ben's both repairs and sells used watches. An employee mistakenly puts the watch in the display case, and Big Ben's sells it to Camilla, who buys it in good faith in the ordinary course. Uncle Deadly sues Camilla. What is the most likely result?
o: Uncle Deadly wins, because he handed over the watch only for cleaning, never for sale.
Camilla wins, because the watch was entrusted to a merchant that deals in watches.
Camilla wins only if Big Ben's sold the watch on purpose rather than by mistake.
Uncle Deadly wins, because Big Ben's had no title to the watch and so could pass none.
The answer depends on whether Uncle Deadly signed a repair ticket limiting Big Ben's rights.
oe: The conditions of the delivery don't matter. Any delivery counts as entrusting (§ 2-403(3)).

Correct. Entrusting goods to a merchant that deals in goods of that kind gives the merchant power to transfer all of the entruster's rights to a buyer in ordinary course (§ 2-403(2)). Entrusting includes any delivery for any purpose, such as repair (§ 2-403(3)).
Section 2-403(2) doesn't depend on the merchant's motive.
Entrustment creates a power to transfer the entruster's rights even though the merchant has no title.
The paperwork for the entrustment doesn't change the result.
topic: Tier 1 · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-403) — Entrustment to a merchant

q: Rowlf sells 50 crystal chandeliers to Camilla, F.O.B. Rowlf's warehouse. Rowlf's employees pack them loosely in thin cardboard with no padding, which falls short of what the trade expects for crystal. Rowlf hands them to a carrier and notifies Camilla. Ordinary bumps in transit shatter most of them. Who bears the loss?
o: Rowlf, because the poorly packed goods didn't conform, so the risk stayed with him.
The carrier, because goods damaged in transit are always the carrier's responsibility.
Camilla, because in an F.O.B. seller's-warehouse contract risk passes on delivery to the carrier.
Camilla, unless the contract expressly required the seller to use special packaging.
Camilla, because she can sue the carrier for damage that happened in transit.
oe: Correct. A shipment-contract seller must make a contract for transportation that is reasonable given the nature of the goods (§ 2-504(a)), and the goods themselves must be adequately packaged (§ 2-314(2)(e)). The tender didn't conform, so under § 2-510(1) the risk stayed on Rowlf. See Problem 4-7(d)(1).
The carrier is liable for its own fault, not for the shipper's packing failures.
Risk passes on delivery to the carrier only after a proper, conforming shipment. A defective tender keeps the risk on the seller under § 2-510(1).
Even with no packaging term, the seller must ship in a manner reasonable for the goods, and merchantability requires adequate packaging.
The carrier isn't liable for damage caused by the shipper's own poor packing, and in any event the risk never passed.
topic: Tier 1 · Risk of loss & identification (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510) — Improper packaging in a shipment contract

q: A sale-of-goods contract contains this conspicuous clause: "THERE ARE NO WARRANTIES WHICH EXTEND BEYOND THE DESCRIPTION ON THE FACE HEREOF." The seller is a merchant, and the goods are unfit for ordinary use. Which implied warranty most clearly survives?
o: Both, because the clause isn't specific enough to exclude any warranty.
Neither, because the clause excludes all warranties.
Fitness for a particular purpose, because the clause excludes only express warranties.
Merchantability, because the clause doesn't mention merchantability.
Title, because only title survives a general disclaimer.
oe: It's the statute's own example for fitness.
It excludes fitness but not merchantability.
The clause is the statutory model for excluding fitness.

Correct. That language is the statute's example of language sufficient to exclude fitness (§ 2-316(2)). Merchantability can be excluded only by language that mentions it, or by an alternative under § 2-316(3).
Title is governed by § 2-312(2) and survives this clause, but the question asks which implied warranty of quality most clearly survives.
topic: Tier 1 · Warranty disclaimers (§ 2-316) — Fitness language leaves merchantability

q: Which of the following is NOT a repudiation of a contract for the sale of goods?
o: A seller's statement that it will deliver only if the buyer agrees to a price increase not required by the contract.
A seller's sale to a third party of the one-of-a-kind goods it had agreed to sell to the buyer.
A seller's failure to tender delivery of the goods on the date its performance is due.
A seller's clear statement, a month before delivery, that it won't deliver.
A buyer's failure to provide adequate assurance within 30 days after receiving a justified demand.
oe: Conditioning performance on a change in terms is a repudiation (§ 2-610 cmt. 2).
Conduct that makes performance impossible is a repudiation (§ 2-610 cmt. 1).
Correct. Failing to perform when performance is due is a breach, not a repudiation. A repudiation is a party's signal before performance is due that it won't perform when required.
This is the classic anticipatory repudiation (§ 2-610).
This is a repudiation under § 2-609(4).
topic: Tier 2 · Insecurity & repudiation (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — What is NOT a repudiation

q: Animal and Gonzo orally agree that Animal will sell Gonzo 100 drumsticks for $1,000. They then orally agree to reduce the order to 40 drumsticks for $400. Nothing is in writing. Is the modified agreement enforceable?
o: No, because the original $1,000 contract was within the statute of frauds.
No, because the modification wasn't supported by any new consideration.
Yes, but only if Gonzo has already paid for the 40 drumsticks.
No, because an oral change to a contract for $500 or more is never enforceable.
Yes, because the contract as modified is for less than $500.
oe: The question is whether the contract as modified is within § 2-201.
Modifications need no consideration under § 2-209(1).
Payment matters to the part-performance exception, which isn't needed here.
Section 2-209 has no such rule. It looks at the contract as modified.
Correct. Section 2-209(3) applies the statute of frauds only if the contract as modified is within its provisions. A $400 contract isn't. See Problem 3-4(b).
topic: Tier 2 · Modification (§ 2-209) — Modification brings the price under $500

q: A landowner agrees to sell a construction company 10,000 tons of gravel from a pit on her land. Under the contract, the landowner will excavate the gravel and load it onto the company's trucks. Is the contract a sale of goods?
o: No, because contracts for minerals are always governed by real property law.
No, because gravel is part of the real property until it's removed.
Yes, but only after the gravel is excavated.
Yes, because minerals are goods when they are to be severed by the seller.
Yes, because anything removable from land is goods no matter who removes it.
oe: That's true only when the buyer is to sever them.
Section 2-107(1) treats it as goods when the seller is to sever it.
Section 2-107(1) characterizes the contract at the time it is made.
Correct. A contract for the sale of minerals "or the like" to be removed from realty is a contract for the sale of goods "if they are to be severed by the seller" (§ 2-107(1)).
For minerals and structures, it matters whether the seller or the buyer severs them (§ 2-107(1)).
topic: Tier 3 · Scope, goods & merchants (§§ 2-102, 2-105, 2-107) — Minerals severed by the seller

q: Gobo contracts to sell Red 100 steel beams. Gobo assigns the contract to another manufacturer, which agrees to perform but never delivers. Red sues Gobo. Gobo argues that once it delegated, it was off the hook. What is the most likely result?
o: Gobo wins, because Red never objected when Gobo assigned the contract to the manufacturer.
Gobo wins, because a valid delegation transfers the duty entirely to the delegate.
Red wins only if the contract prohibited Gobo from delegating its duties.
Red may sue only the manufacturer, which took over the contract and promised to perform it.
Red wins, because delegating doesn't relieve Gobo of its duty or liability.
oe: Red's failure to object doesn't release Gobo. Only a novation, which requires Red's agreement, would do that.
Delegation adds a party who owes the performance but doesn't release the original party.
Gobo remains liable whether or not delegation was permitted.
Red may sue the delegate, but it doesn't lose its claim against Gobo.
Correct. "No delegation of performance relieves the party delegating of any duty to perform or any liability for breach" (§ 2-210(1)). See Problem 6-2(c).
topic: Tier 2 · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210) — Delegating party stays liable

q: Zoot, a saxophone importer, buys 100 saxophones from a European maker "C.I.F. Port of Baltimore." The maker loads them on a ship, buys a proper insurance policy for Zoot's benefit, pays the freight, and sends Zoot the documents. The ship sinks in a storm. Must Zoot pay the price?
o: Yes, because a C.I.F. contract is a shipment contract, so risk passed on shipment.
No, because a C.I.F. contract means no arrival, no sale, and the saxophones never arrived.
No, because naming the destination port makes a C.I.F. contract a destination contract.
No, because the seller paid for insurance, which shows it kept the risk during transit.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Under a C.I.F. term the price includes cost, insurance, and freight to the named destination, but the seller's obligation is to ship and to tender the documents, including insurance for the buyer's benefit (§ 2-320). Risk passes on shipment, and the buyer's protection is the insurance policy.
"No arrival, no sale" is a separate term (§ 2-324). It isn't implied by C.I.F.
C.I.F. destination is a shipment term. The named port only fixes the price components.
The seller buys insurance for the buyer's benefit precisely because the buyer bears the risk in transit.
One of the other choices is correct: Yes, because a C.I.F. contract is a shipment contract, so risk passed on shipment.
topic: Tier 1 · Risk of loss & identification (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510) — C.I.F. term

q: When Gonzo takes delivery of a used cabin cruiser, he sees the GPS doesn't work. The seller makes no promise to fix it, and Gonzo accepts the boat anyway. A month later, frustrated with the GPS, he tries to revoke his acceptance because of it. What is the most likely result?
o: He may revoke only if the seller is a merchant that regularly deals in boats.
He can't revoke because of the GPS, but he may still recover damages for it.
He can't revoke, and he has no remedy of any kind, because he accepted the boat.
He may revoke, because a broken GPS substantially impairs the value of a cabin cruiser.
He may revoke, because a buyer may revoke within a reasonable time after delivery for any defect.
oe: The seller's merchant status doesn't control revocation.

Correct. Acceptance with knowledge of a nonconformity can't be revoked because of it unless acceptance was on the reasonable assumption that it would be seasonably cured (§§ 2-607(2), 2-608(1)(a)). Acceptance doesn't impair other remedies for the nonconformity, but the buyer must notify the seller of the breach within a reasonable time (§ 2-607(3)(a)).
Acceptance doesn't bar a damages claim for the known defect.
Even if it does, a buyer who accepts with knowledge and no expectation of cure can't revoke for that defect.
Revocation has specific conditions under § 2-608(1), and Gonzo meets neither.
topic: Tier 2 · Tender, inspection, acceptance & payment — Revocation for a known defect

q: A distributor sues its supplier with a single claim: that the supplier "breached the duty of good faith" by being curt and uncooperative in meetings. The distributor doesn't point to any contract term whose performance or enforcement was affected. What is the most likely result?
o: The claim fails, because good faith can be disclaimed by agreement and was disclaimed here.
The claim fails, because the parties' contract didn't expressly mention good faith.
The claim succeeds, because every contract governed by the UCC imposes a duty of good faith.
The claim fails, because good faith doesn't create a claim apart from the contract's terms.
The claim succeeds if the supplier fell below reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing.
oe: Good faith can't be disclaimed (§ 1-302(b)), and nothing suggests a disclaimer.
The obligation is imposed by law in every contract. The problem is the lack of a connection to any term.
The duty exists, but it works through specific contract obligations, not as a free-standing claim.

Correct. Every contract imposes an obligation of good faith "in its performance and enforcement" (§ 1-304). Comment 1 explains that the doctrine doesn't support an independent cause of action for failure to perform or enforce in good faith. It operates through the contract's terms.
Fair dealing is part of the definition of good faith (§ 1-201(b)(20)), but it still must attach to performing or enforcing a term.
topic: Tier 3 · Good faith, variation & unconscionability — Good faith isn't a stand-alone claim

q: A contract for $20,000 of store display racks provides that the seller will pay $50,000 for each day of late delivery. The buyer's realistic losses from a short delay were small and easy to calculate. The racks arrive two days late, and the buyer sues for $100,000. What is the most likely result?
o: The buyer recovers nothing, because the penalty clause voids the entire contract.
The buyer recovers $100,000, because the seller is a merchant.
The court will reduce the clause to the largest amount that would be reasonable.
The buyer recovers $100,000, because the parties agreed to the amount.
The clause is void as a penalty, and the buyer may recover its actual damages.
oe: Only the penalty term is void.
Merchant status doesn't validate a penalty.
Article 2 voids an unreasonably large term instead of rewriting it.
Freedom of contract doesn't extend to penalties.
Correct. "A term fixing unreasonably large liquidated damages is void as a penalty" (§ 2-718(1)). With the clause out, the buyer may recover ordinary Article 2 damages.
topic: Tier 2 · Remedies & remedy limits (§§ 2-715, 2-718, 2-719) — Liquidated damages as a penalty

q: Before buying a used box truck from a dealer, Fozzie spends an hour going over it as thoroughly as he wants. He sees obvious rust on the frame. Two weeks later, the transmission fails because of internal wear that no ordinary inspection would have revealed. The contract contains no disclaimer. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Fozzie's examination excludes implied warranties as to the rust, but not as to the transmission.
Fozzie keeps implied warranties as to the rust only, because rust is a safety defect.
Fozzie's examination excludes all implied warranties.
Fozzie's examination excludes nothing, because there was no written disclaimer.
Fozzie keeps implied warranties as to both defects, because the seller didn't demand an inspection.
oe: Correct. When the buyer has examined the goods as fully as desired before contracting, there's no implied warranty "with regard to defects which an examination ought in the circumstances to have revealed" (§ 2-316(3)(b)). Hidden internal wear isn't such a defect.
The test is whether the inspection ought to have revealed the defect, not how serious it is.
An examination excludes warranties only as to defects it ought to have revealed.
Section 2-316(3)(b) works without any disclaimer language.
A demand is needed only when the buyer refuses to inspect. Fozzie actually inspected.
topic: Tier 1 · Warranty disclaimers (§ 2-316) — Examination: patent vs. latent defects

q: Under an 18-month supply contract between merchants, a buyer pays three invoices late, and the seller accepts each late payment without protest. The buyer then loses its largest customer and starts missing payments to other suppliers. The seller demands adequate assurance. The buyer argues the seller waived the right by accepting the late payments. What is the most likely result?
o: The buyer wins, because the course of performance changed the payment terms to allow late payment.
The buyer wins, because a party may demand assurance only after the other side actually breaches.
The seller may demand assurance only if the contract expressly gives it a right to do so.
The seller must first reject a late payment before it can demand any assurance from the buyer.
The seller may demand assurance, because accepting late payments doesn't waive that right.
oe: Even if late payment became acceptable, the new facts give fresh grounds for insecurity, and § 2-609(3) preserves the right to demand assurance.
A demand requires reasonable grounds for insecurity, not an actual breach.
The right comes from the statute.
Section 2-609(3) says the opposite.

Correct. "Acceptance of any improper delivery or payment does not prejudice the aggrieved party's right to demand adequate assurance of future performance" (§ 2-609(3)). Between merchants, the reasonableness of the grounds is judged by commercial standards (§ 2-609(2)).
topic: Tier 2 · Insecurity & repudiation (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Accepting late payments doesn't waive assurance

q: On January 2, Gonzo's Feed & Seed, a merchant, emails Camilla a signed offer: "We will sell you 200 bags of chicken feed at $18 a bag. This offer will remain open until July 1." Camilla gives no consideration. On April 15, Gonzo's emails Camilla revoking the offer. On April 20, Camilla emails her acceptance. Is there a contract?
o: No, because irrevocability ended after three months, so the April 15 revocation worked.
Yes, because an email can't be a signed record, so the revocation had no effect.
Yes, because the offer stated that it would remain open until July 1.
No, because a firm offer is binding only if the offeree gives consideration for it.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A merchant's signed firm offer is irrevocable for the time stated, "but in no event may such period of irrevocability exceed three months" (§ 2-205). After April 2, the offer became revocable, and it was revoked before Camilla accepted.
An email from a business account can be a signed record, and a revocation needs no signature.
The stated time exceeds the three-month cap, so irrevocability ended after three months.
A merchant's firm offer under § 2-205 needs no consideration.
One of the other choices is correct: No, because irrevocability ended after three months, so the April 15 revocation worked.
topic: Tier 3 · Formation, firm offers & § 2-207 — Firm offer longer than three months

q: Sweetums sells a bandstand riser to Dr. Teeth's nightclub, "F.O.B. Buyer's loading dock." The carrier arrives at the dock at 10 a.m. on a weekday, as scheduled, and tells the club the riser is ready to unload. The club's manager says the staff is busy and asks the driver to wait in the lot until the next morning. Overnight, the truck is struck by lightning and the riser is destroyed. Who bears the loss?
o: Sweetums, because a merchant seller bears the risk until the buyer actually receives the goods.
Sweetums, because in a destination contract risk passes only when the buyer takes the goods.
The carrier, because it agreed to keep the riser on its truck overnight.
Sweetums, because the riser was still in the carrier's possession when it was destroyed.
The club, because the riser was duly tendered at the destination at a reasonable hour.
oe: The merchant receipt rule in § 2-509(3) applies only when goods are not shipped by carrier or held by a bailee.
The trigger is due tender at the destination, not the buyer's receipt.
The carrier's liability is a separate matter. As between seller and buyer, the risk had passed.
Who has physical possession doesn't decide it. Once due tender was made at the destination, risk passed even though the riser stayed on the truck.

Correct. In a destination contract, risk passes when the goods are "duly so tendered as to enable the buyer to take delivery" there (§ 2-509(1)(b)). The carrier held the riser at the dock at a reasonable hour with notice. The club's choice not to unload doesn't keep the risk on the seller.
topic: Tier 1 · Risk of loss & identification (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510) — Destination contract; buyer delays taking delivery

q: A contract for a commercial ice-cream freezer limits the buyer's remedy to repair or replacement of defective parts, which the contract says is exclusive. The freezer fails repeatedly, and after six repair attempts over four months it still won't hold temperature. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The failure of the remedy automatically voids any separate exclusion of consequential damages.
The remedy has failed of its essential purpose, so other Article 2 remedies are available.
The buyer may now recover only the price of the freezer, and no other damages.
The buyer is limited to more repair attempts, because it agreed to an exclusive remedy.
The limitation was void from the start, because remedy limits aren't allowed in commercial sales.
oe: Many courts, as in Razor v. Hyundai, treat the consequential-damages exclusion separately, judged by unconscionability.

Correct. "Where circumstances cause an exclusive or limited remedy to fail of its essential purpose, remedy may be had as provided in this Act" (§ 2-719(2)). A repair remedy that can't produce a working machine within a reasonable time fails of its essential purpose.
Once the remedy fails, the buyer may seek its full Article 2 remedies, subject to any separate valid exclusion.
An exclusive remedy that fails of its essential purpose no longer limits the buyer.
Section 2-719(1) expressly permits limited remedies.
topic: Tier 2 · Remedies & remedy limits (§§ 2-715, 2-718, 2-719) — Repair remedy fails of its essential purpose

q: Uncle Deadly leaves his antique pocket watch with Big Ben's Jewelers, which repairs and sells used watches, for cleaning. Big Ben's owes Camilla, a watch wholesaler, $5,000 from an earlier transaction, and it hands her Uncle Deadly's watch to reduce that debt. Camilla doesn't know the watch belongs to someone else. Who has the better claim to the watch?
o: Uncle Deadly, because the entrustment rule protects only consumers who buy at retail.
Camilla, because Big Ben's is a merchant that deals in watches of that kind.
Uncle Deadly, because taking goods to satisfy a debt isn't buying in ordinary course.
Camilla, because she took the watch in good faith without knowing of anyone else's claim.
Camilla, because accepting the watch in satisfaction of a debt is giving value for it.
oe: Merchants can be buyers in ordinary course. Camilla fails because of how she acquired the watch.
The merchant's status is necessary but not enough. The buyer must also qualify.

Correct. The entrustment power runs only to a buyer in ordinary course of business (§ 2-403(2)). The definition excludes a person who acquires goods "in total or partial satisfaction of a money debt" (§ 1-201(b)(9)).
Good faith isn't enough. She must also be a buyer in ordinary course, and taking goods to satisfy a debt disqualifies her.
Value matters for good-faith purchasers under § 2-403(1). Here the question is buyer-in-ordinary-course status under § 2-403(2).
topic: Tier 1 · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-403) — Entrustment: not a buyer in ordinary course

q: Unless otherwise agreed, which of the following is NOT one of the seller's duties when the contract requires or authorizes it to ship goods by carrier but doesn't require delivery at a particular destination?
o: Make a contract for transportation that is reasonable given the nature of the goods.
Obtain and promptly deliver any document the buyer needs to obtain possession.
Put the goods in the possession of a carrier.
Buy insurance covering the goods during transit for the buyer's benefit.
Promptly notify the buyer of the shipment.
oe: This is required by § 2-504(a).
This is required by § 2-504(b).
This is required by § 2-504(a).
Correct. Section 2-504 doesn't require the seller to insure. That duty arises only from a term like C.I.F. (§ 2-320).
This is required by § 2-504(c).
topic: Tier 1 · Risk of loss & identification (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510) — Seller's shipping duties: which is NOT required

q: Kermit, a seller, "assigns all my rights under this contract" to Fozzie, who accepts the assignment. Nothing indicates the parties meant to transfer only rights. Fozzie never delivers the goods. Whom may the buyer sue for nondelivery?
o: Either Kermit or Fozzie, because both are now bound to deliver the goods.
Only Kermit, because an assignment of "rights" never transfers duties.
Only Kermit, because the buyer never contracted with Fozzie.
Neither, because the buyer didn't consent to the assignment.
Only Fozzie, because Kermit transferred the contract to him.
oe: Correct. A general assignment of "all my rights under the contract" is also a delegation of performance unless the language or circumstances indicate otherwise, and the assignee's acceptance is a promise to perform that the other party can enforce (§ 2-210(5)). Kermit stays liable (§ 2-210(1)).
Section 2-210(5) treats a general assignment as a delegation too.
The assignee's acceptance creates a promise the other party may enforce (§ 2-210(5)).
Consent isn't required for an assignment and delegation that is otherwise permitted.
Delegation never relieves the delegating party (§ 2-210(1)).
topic: Tier 2 · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210) — Assignee's acceptance is a promise to perform

q: Lew Zealand buys a used sailboat. When he asks whether it's ready for an ocean crossing, the seller says, "She's seaworthy." On the first offshore passage, the hull leaks badly through a long-standing crack. The seller argues "seaworthy" was mere puffing. What is the most likely result?
o: Lew wins, but only if the seller is a boat dealer and not a private owner.
The seller wins, because the statement was about how the boat would perform in the future.
The seller wins, because Lew could have hired a marine surveyor before he bought.
Lew wins, because "seaworthy" asserts a fact about the boat's condition.
The seller wins, because one-word statements are too general to be warranties.
oe: Any seller can make an express warranty.
A statement about present condition is a fact. Even promises about the goods' future performance can be warranties.
The buyer's chance to inspect doesn't automatically defeat an express warranty.
Correct. "Seaworthy" describes a specific, verifiable condition, and it was given in response to an inquiry. Those factors point toward a warranty rather than commendation. See Problem 3-5(h).
Length doesn't matter. The question is whether the statement asserts a fact about the goods.
topic: Tier 1 · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Specific condition term ("seaworthy")

q: Two merchants are drafting a sale contract. Which of the following Article 2 rules could they NOT change by agreement?
o: When the risk of loss passes from seller to buyer under § 2-509.
The court's power under § 2-302 to refuse to enforce an unconscionable clause.
The place of delivery under § 2-308, which applies when the contract doesn't say where.
The buyer's right under § 2-513 to inspect the goods before paying for them.
The time for payment under § 2-310, which ties payment to the buyer's receipt.
oe: Section 2-509(4) says its rules are subject to contrary agreement.
Correct. Parties can't contract out of a court's power to police unconscionability. The other provisions are default rules that apply "unless otherwise agreed." See Problem 5-1(b).
Section 2-308 applies "unless otherwise agreed."
Section 2-513(1) applies "unless otherwise agreed."
Section 2-310 applies "unless otherwise agreed."
topic: Tier 3 · Good faith, variation & unconscionability — Which rule can't be varied by agreement

q: A signed purchase agreement for a commercial oven sets out the model, price, and quantity and is intended as final on those terms. It says nothing about installation and has no merger clause. The buyer offers evidence that, before signing, the seller orally agreed to install the oven at no charge. Is the evidence admissible?
o: No, because free installation contradicts the price term, which was final in the writing.
Yes, because the parol evidence rule applies only to prior written agreements, not oral ones.
Probably yes, as a consistent additional term, unless the writing was meant to be complete and exclusive.
Yes, but only if the writing is ambiguous about whether installation was included in the price.
No, because a prior oral agreement can never be used to add a term to a signed written contract.
oe: Silence on installation isn't a contradiction. The term adds something the writing doesn't address.
It applies to prior agreements and contemporaneous oral agreements.

Correct. A writing that is final as to the terms it includes may be supplemented by consistent additional terms (§ 2-202(b)), unless it was intended as complete and exclusive. Comment 3 also excludes terms that, if agreed, would certainly have been included in the document.
Article 2 doesn't require ambiguity before admitting consistent additional terms (§ 2-202 cmt. 1(c)).
Section 2-202(b) allows consistent additional terms to supplement a partial integration.
topic: Tier 2 · Parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) — Partial integration; consistent additional term

q: A signed contract between two produce merchants requires delivery of lettuce "by 12:00 noon on Friday." In the regional produce trade, "Friday delivery" customarily means any time before 5 p.m. The seller delivers at 3 p.m., and the buyer rejects as late. Who is right?
o: The seller, because a three-hour delay is trivial and the lettuce arrived the same day.
The seller, because usage of trade defines what the parties' words mean in their trade.
The buyer, because an express term controls when it can't be squared with a trade usage.
Neither, because the conflicting terms knock each other out and a gap filler applies.
The seller, because both parties are merchants in the same trade and bound by its usages.
oe: Under perfect tender, a buyer may reject for any nonconformity, including time (§ 2-601).
Usage can explain or supplement terms, but it can't contradict a specific express term.

Correct. Express terms, course of performance, course of dealing, and usage of trade are read consistently where reasonable. Where they can't be, express terms prevail (§ 1-303(e)(1)). "By 12:00 noon" can't be read as "before 5 p.m."
The knockout idea applies to conflicting forms under § 2-207, not to an express term versus trade usage.
Being in the trade binds them to usages, but usages still yield to express terms.
topic: Tier 2 · Course of performance, waiver & estoppel (§ 1-303) — Express term beats trade usage

q: A signed record shows that Scooter will sell Rowlf 100 piano benches for $10,000. The parties later orally agree that Scooter will deliver 110 benches for the same total price. Scooter delivers only 100, and Rowlf sues for the other 10. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The extra 10 are enforceable, because the total price stayed the same after the change.
The extra 10 are enforceable, because the original signed record satisfies the statute of frauds.
The extra 10 are enforceable, because modifications need no consideration under § 2-209.
The statute of frauds likely bars the extra 10, because the writing shows only 100.
The whole contract is unenforceable, because the parties modified it orally.
oe: The quantity limit in § 2-201(1) applies whatever the price.
The original writing shows 100, and it can't support enforcement of 110.
The issue is the statute of frauds, not consideration.

Correct. A contract as modified within § 2-201 must satisfy it (§ 2-209(3)), and a writing doesn't support enforcement "beyond the quantity of goods shown in such writing" (§ 2-201(1)). See Problem 3-4(c).
The writing still supports enforcement up to the 100 benches it shows.
topic: Tier 2 · Modification (§ 2-209) — Oral increase beyond the quantity in the writing

q: A weaver buys five lots of "Magenta No. 2" yarn from a mill. The lots differ noticeably in shade, so a blanket knit from more than one lot looks striped. The mill says the variation comes from natural differences in fiber and dyeing. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The weaver has a fitness claim, because knitting single-color blankets is a particular purpose.
The weaver has a claim only if the mill gave an express warranty that every lot would match.
The weaver has no claim, because variation caused by natural differences in fiber is never a breach.
The weaver has no claim, because each lot, considered by itself, is of even color and merchantable.
The weaver may have a merchantability claim, unless the variation is within what the agreement or trade allows.
oe: Using yarn to knit consistent-looking goods is an ordinary purpose, and nothing shows reliance on the mill's selection.
The even-quality standard is part of the implied warranty. No express warranty is needed.
The cause of a variation isn't a defense if the goods fall outside permitted variations.
The standard applies "among all units involved," not just within each lot.

Correct. Merchantable goods must "run, within the variations permitted by the agreement, of even kind, quality and quantity within each unit and among all units involved" (§ 2-314(2)(d)). Trade usage can define the permitted variation (§ 1-303(c)).
topic: Tier 1 · Implied warranties (§§ 2-314, 2-315) — Uneven kind and quality among units

q: A signed contract describes the goods as "one 2019 Grover-Lift forklift, in good working condition," and later says, "SOLD AS IS." The forklift doesn't run. Which statement is most accurate?
o: "As is" excludes every warranty, express or implied, so the buyer has no claim.
The express warranty survives, because "as is" excludes only implied warranties.
No warranty exists, because "good working condition" is too vague to be a warranty.
The two terms cancel each other out, so neither one applies and gap fillers govern.
The later term controls, because it appears after the description in the writing.
oe: Section 2-316(3)(a) is limited to implied warranties.

Correct. "As is" excludes implied warranties (§ 2-316(3)(a)). Words creating an express warranty and words negating it are read consistently if possible, and otherwise the negation is inoperative to the extent unreasonable (§ 2-316(1)).
Saying a machine works is an affirmation of fact about it.
Article 2 resolves this conflict in favor of the express warranty under § 2-316(1).
Placement doesn't decide it. Section 2-316(1) favors the express warranty.
topic: Tier 1 · Warranty disclaimers (§ 2-316) — "As is" vs. an express description

q: In each of eight earlier sales of pressure gauges to a refinery, a supplier included a certificate showing that each gauge had been calibrated before shipment. The ninth order says nothing about certificates, and the supplier ships uncalibrated gauges without them. The refinery's strongest argument is that the supplier breached:
o: The implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose.
No warranty, because the ninth order was silent about calibration.
An implied warranty arising from course of performance under this contract.
An implied warranty arising from course of dealing under § 2-314(3).
An express warranty by sample, because earlier gauges were calibrated.
oe: Nothing shows a particular purpose or the refinery's reliance on the supplier's selection.
Course of dealing supplements an agreement that is silent on a point (§ 1-303(d)).
Course of performance is repeated performance under one contract. The earlier sales were separate transactions, which makes them a course of dealing.

Correct. Section 2-314(3) recognizes "other implied warranties" that "arise from course of dealing or usage of trade." Eight earlier sales with calibration certificates are a course of dealing (§ 1-303(b)) that gives meaning to and supplements the ninth contract.
Earlier deliveries under other contracts weren't samples for this one.
topic: Tier 1 · Implied warranties (§§ 2-314, 2-315) — Implied warranty from course of dealing

q: A seller of used forklifts invites buyers to "look around the lot." Waldorf buys one without examining it at all. The seller never asked him to examine it. It turns out to have a cracked mast that a quick look would have revealed. The seller argues Waldorf lost his implied warranties by refusing to examine. Is the seller right?
o: Yes, because inviting buyers to look around the lot is a demand that they examine the goods.
No, because a buyer's examination of the goods never has any effect on implied warranties.
No, because failing to inspect isn't a refusal unless the seller demanded an inspection.
Yes, because used forklifts are sold without implied warranties unless the seller gives one.
Yes, because a quick look at the forklift would have revealed the cracked mast to anyone.
oe: A general invitation isn't a demand that this buyer examine these goods.
Examination or refusal after a demand can exclude warranties as to defects that inspection ought to reveal (§ 2-316(3)(b)).
Correct. Comment 8 to § 2-316 explains that a buyer doesn't refuse to examine merely by not doing so. The seller must demand that the buyer examine the goods fully. See Problem 5-3.
Used goods sold by a merchant carry the merchantability warranty, adjusted to their age and condition.
Without a demand, the buyer's failure to look doesn't exclude the warranty.
topic: Tier 1 · Warranty disclaimers (§ 2-316) — No inspection without a demand

q: A restaurant-supply company's preprinted sales form says: "This agreement may be modified only by a writing signed by both parties." A restaurant, also a merchant, signs the form only at the bottom. Later, the supplier's sales manager orally agrees to cut the price by 10%. When the supplier bills the full price, the restaurant argues that the oral price cut is binding because it never separately signed the clause. What is the most likely result?
o: The oral price cut is binding, because the restaurant never separately signed the no-oral-modification clause.
The oral price cut is binding, because a modification under Article 2 needs no new consideration.
The oral price cut is binding, because the sales manager had actual authority to set the prices.
The clause is unenforceable, because a merchant can't bind another party with terms on its own form.
The clause binds the restaurant, so the oral cut fails as a modification but may operate as a waiver.
oe: Separate signature is required only when the other party is a non-merchant.
Consideration isn't the problem. The no-oral-modification clause is.
Authority doesn't overcome a valid no-oral-modification clause.
Between merchants, the clause on one party's form binds a party that signed the form.

Correct. A signed agreement excluding modification except by a signed writing can't be otherwise modified, and the requirement that the other party separately sign it applies only "except as between merchants" (§ 2-209(2)). The failed modification can still work as a waiver (§ 2-209(4)).
topic: Tier 2 · Modification (§ 2-209) — No-oral-modification clause between merchants

q: A seller of a used piano makes a statement about the piano, and the buyer later claims it was an express warranty. Which fact most strongly supports treating the statement as an affirmation of fact rather than an opinion?
o: The statement was made orally, in conversation, rather than in writing.
The seller volunteered the statement on its own, without the buyer asking about anything.
The statement described the piano's overall quality in general, glowing terms.
The seller said it in response to the buyer's specific question about that feature.
The seller qualified the statement with words like "I think" and "probably."
oe: Oral statements can be warranties, but a writing is generally stronger evidence of a factual commitment. Being oral doesn't support warranty treatment.
Volunteered statements are more likely to be seen as sales talk.
General statements point toward puffing.

Correct. Statements made in response to an inquiry are more likely to be taken as warranties than freely volunteered praise. Specificity, measurability, and the reasonableness of relying on the statement also point that way.
Hedged or equivocal statements point toward opinion.
topic: Tier 1 · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Factors: fact vs. opinion

q: A written contract for 10,000 yards of carpet yarn says: "This document contains all the terms of the parties' agreement and is the complete and exclusive statement of their agreement." In a dispute, the buyer offers three kinds of evidence. Which is admissible to supplement the writing?
o: Evidence of a prior oral agreement adding a consistent term.
None of the evidence, because a merger clause bars all extrinsic evidence.
Evidence of a contemporaneous oral agreement adding a consistent term.
Evidence of a prior written agreement that contradicts a term in the contract.
Evidence of a consistent usage of trade in the carpet industry.
oe: A complete and exclusive writing excludes consistent additional terms (§ 2-202(b)).
A merger clause doesn't bar course of dealing, usage of trade, or course of performance.
Contemporaneous oral terms are excluded just like prior ones.
Contradictory prior agreements are excluded by any final writing.

Correct. Even a complete and exclusive writing may be explained or supplemented by course of dealing, usage of trade, and course of performance (§ 2-202(a)). Only subsection (b), on consistent additional terms, is cut off by complete integration. See Problem 5-12(a).
topic: Tier 2 · Parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) — Complete integration; trade usage still in

q: Grover agrees to buy a specific antique carousel horse from a merchant seller, to be picked up next week. Before pickup, a storm leaks through the seller's roof and the water damages the horse's paint without either party's fault. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Grover may accept the horse at the full price and also sue the seller for the cost of repainting.
Grover may avoid the contract or take the horse at a reduced price, with no further claim.
Grover must pay the full price, because the horse was identified when the contract was made.
The contract is automatically avoided, because the horse was damaged before risk passed.
None of the above.
oe: When accepting with an allowance, the buyer has no further right against the seller.

Correct. When identified goods suffer a partial casualty without fault before risk passes, the buyer may demand inspection and either avoid the contract or accept the goods "with due allowance from the contract price for the deterioration" but "without further right against the seller" (§ 2-613(b)).
Risk hadn't passed, because a merchant seller keeps the risk until the buyer receives the goods (§ 2-509(3)).
Automatic avoidance applies only to a total loss (§ 2-613(a)).
One of the other choices is correct: Grover may avoid the contract or take the horse at a reduced price, with no further claim.
topic: Tier 2 · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-615) — Partial casualty to identified goods

q: A contract requires 10,000 widgets a month for 12 months, delivered by the 5th of each month. The April shipment arrives April 7, and the buyer accepts it without complaint. In May, the seller again delivers on the 7th and argues that the parties' course of performance has moved the deadline to the 7th. Is the seller right?
o: Yes, because the buyer accepted a late delivery without complaining and so agreed to the new date.
Yes, because the seller relied on the buyer's acceptance when it scheduled the May delivery.
No, because one late delivery isn't a course of performance, though it may waive that delay.
Yes, because accepting the April delivery late modified the contract's delivery deadline.
No, because a course of performance can never change an express term such as a delivery date.
oe: One acceptance doesn't show the repeated pattern § 1-303(a) requires.
Nothing shows detrimental reliance, and reliance wouldn't create a course of performance anyway.

Correct. A course of performance requires repeated occasions for performance accepted or acquiesced in without objection (§ 1-303(a)). One late delivery isn't enough. Accepting it may waive that one breach. See Problem 3-5(A).
Nothing suggests the parties agreed to change the deadline. Silent acceptance of one late shipment isn't a modification.
Course of performance can show a waiver or modification of a term (§ 1-303(f)). It just requires more than one occasion.
topic: Tier 2 · Course of performance, waiver & estoppel (§ 1-303) — A single occasion isn't a course of performance

q: Which of the following statements about unconscionability under § 2-302 is NOT accurate?
o: The jury decides whether a clause is unconscionable, judged as of the time of the breach.
A court may enforce the rest of the contract without the unconscionable clause.
The parties must be given a reasonable opportunity to present evidence of the clause's commercial setting, purpose, and effect.
A court may refuse to enforce the entire contract.
A court may limit the application of an unconscionable clause to avoid an unconscionable result.
oe: Correct. Unconscionability is decided by the court "as a matter of law" and is judged "at the time it was made," not at the time of breach (§ 2-302(1)).
This is one option under § 2-302(1).
This is required by § 2-302(2).
This is one option under § 2-302(1).
This is one option under § 2-302(1).
topic: Tier 3 · Good faith, variation & unconscionability — Unconscionability: which is NOT accurate

q: Kermit, a frog who plays banjo as a hobby, is selling his old banjo. Scooter tells him, "I play outdoor gigs on the bayou. I need one that holds its tuning in heavy humidity. Pick one for me." Kermit hands him the banjo and says, "This is the one you want." Scooter buys it. It goes badly out of tune in humid weather, though it plays fine indoors. Which claim is Scooter most likely to win?
o: Both merchantability and fitness for a particular purpose.
Breach of the implied warranty of merchantability.
Neither, because implied warranties arise only when the seller is a merchant.
Breach of the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose.
Neither, because Scooter didn't put his needs in writing.
oe: Merchantability fails because Kermit isn't a merchant with respect to banjos.
Kermit isn't a merchant who deals in banjos, so no merchantability warranty arises (§ 2-314(1)). And the banjo works for ordinary indoor use.
That limit applies only to merchantability. The fitness warranty doesn't require a merchant seller.
Correct. Kermit knew Scooter's particular purpose and that Scooter was relying on Kermit's judgment to select a suitable banjo. Under § 2-315 any seller, merchant or not, can make this warranty.
Section 2-315 doesn't require a writing. The seller need only have reason to know the purpose and the buyer's reliance.
topic: Tier 1 · Implied warranties (§§ 2-314, 2-315) — Fitness warranty by a non-merchant

q: Animal leaves his drum kit with a recording studio while he tours. The studio rents out equipment but doesn't sell drums. The studio sells the kit to a buyer who pays fair value in good faith. Animal sues the buyer. What is the most likely result?
o: Animal wins, because the studio doesn't deal in drums and so had no power to sell his kit.
The buyer wins, because the studio is a merchant in the music business.
Animal wins, but only if he can prove the studio acted in bad faith.
The buyer wins, because Animal voluntarily handed over possession of the kit to the studio.
The buyer wins, because he was a good-faith purchaser who paid fair value for the kit.
oe: Correct. Section 2-403(2) gives the power to transfer only to "a merchant who deals in goods of that kind." A studio that rents but doesn't sell drums doesn't qualify, and the studio had no voidable title under § 2-403(1) either.
It must deal in goods of the kind sold, which here means drums.
The studio's state of mind doesn't matter. It lacked the power to transfer.
Voluntary delivery to a non-dealer doesn't trigger the entrustment rule.
A good-faith purchaser takes no more than the transferor had or could transfer, and the studio had neither title nor power.
topic: Tier 1 · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-403) — Entrustment to a non-dealer

q: A small regional mill agrees to supply all the grain requirements of Oscar's Bakery, a single neighborhood shop. Oscar sells his business and assigns his rights under the contract to a national bakery chain whose requirements are 400 times as large. The mill objects. Is the assignment effective?
o: No, because it would materially change the mill's duty and increase its burden.
Yes, because a national chain is far more likely than Oscar to pay its bills on time.
Yes, because the contract between the mill and Oscar contains no anti-assignment clause.
Yes, because contract rights can always be assigned without the other party's consent.
No, because requirements contracts can never be assigned to anyone.
oe: Correct. Rights can be assigned "except where the assignment would materially change the duty of the other party, or increase materially the burden or risk imposed on him by his contract" (§ 2-210(2)). A requirements contract measured by a national chain is a vastly different obligation.
The question is the effect on the mill's duty and risk, not the assignee's creditworthiness alone.
Even without a clause, § 2-210(2) bars an assignment that materially changes the other party's duty.
The general freedom to assign is subject to the material-change limit in § 2-210(2).
They can, if the assignment doesn't materially change the other party's obligations.
topic: Tier 2 · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210) — Assignment that materially increases risk

q: A law office receives a new copier that keeps jamming. The office promptly emails the seller that it rejects the copier and asks the seller to pick it up. While waiting, the office keeps using the copier for all its daily work for three weeks. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The rejection stands, because the office notified the seller promptly after delivery.
The seller may treat the office's continued use as an acceptance of the copier.
The office has accepted only the copies it made, not the copier itself.
The rejection stands, because the copier was defective, so the office had a right to reject.
The office has revoked its rejection, so it must pay the full price and loses its damages claim.
oe: A timely notice doesn't protect a buyer who then treats the goods as its own.

Correct. After rejection, any exercise of ownership by the buyer is wrongful (§ 2-602(2)(a)), and doing any act inconsistent with the seller's ownership is an acceptance, at the seller's option if it's wrongful against the seller (§ 2-606(1)(c)).
Acceptance under § 2-606 is of the goods, and part of a commercial unit can't be accepted alone (§ 2-606(2)).
A rightful reason to reject doesn't permit the buyer to keep using the goods.
If the use is treated as acceptance, the office must pay the price (§ 2-607(1)) but keeps its claim for damages for the defect if it gives notice (§§ 2-607(3), 2-714).
topic: Tier 2 · Tender, inspection, acceptance & payment — Use after rejection

q: On March 1, a hotel mails a sign maker an offer: "Make and deliver 50 custom brass room signs at $40 each; delivery by May 1." The offer doesn't specify how to accept. The sign maker begins making the signs but never tells the hotel. By April 10, having heard nothing, the hotel orders signs elsewhere and tells the sign maker the offer is withdrawn. The sign maker says it accepted by beginning work. What is the most likely result?
o: The sign maker wins, because the signs are specially manufactured goods made for the hotel.
The sign maker wins, because the hotel's offer was irrevocable until the May 1 delivery date.
The hotel may treat the offer as lapsed, because the sign maker never notified it.
The hotel wins, because an offer to buy goods can be accepted only by a return promise.
The sign maker wins, because beginning the requested performance is a valid acceptance.
oe: That exception concerns the statute of frauds, not whether a contract was formed.
Nothing made the offer a firm offer under § 2-205.

Correct. Where the beginning of a requested performance is a reasonable mode of acceptance, "an offeror who is not notified of acceptance within a reasonable time may treat the offer as having lapsed before acceptance" (§ 2-206(2)). Six weeks of silence on a two-month job is likely more than reasonable.
Unless the offer says otherwise, it may be accepted in any reasonable manner (§ 2-206(1)(a)), including by beginning performance.
It can be, but § 2-206(2) adds the notice requirement.
topic: Tier 3 · Formation, firm offers & § 2-207 — Beginning performance without notifying the offeror

q: An ice-cream shop buys a commercial freezer under a contract that makes repair or replacement of defective parts the exclusive remedy and also says, conspicuously, "SELLER IS NOT LIABLE FOR CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES." After six failed repair attempts, the repair remedy has failed of its essential purpose. The shop lost $18,000 of inventory and sales while the freezer was down. Under the approach in Razor v. Hyundai, can the buyer recover the $18,000?
o: Yes, because the failure of the repair remedy knocks out every limitation in the contract.
Probably not, because the exclusion stands on its own unless it's unconscionable.
Yes, because the exclusion wasn't in a separate document signed by the shop.
No, because consequential damages are never recoverable for a breach of warranty.
Yes, because a clause excluding consequential damages is always unconscionable.
oe: That's the dependent approach some courts take, but not the one in Razor.

Correct. Under the independent approach in Razor, the failure of a limited remedy under § 2-719(2) doesn't automatically knock out a separate exclusion of consequential damages, which is enforceable unless unconscionable (§ 2-719(3)). Commercial losses between businesses are rarely excluded unconscionably.
No separate signature is required.
Consequential damages are recoverable under § 2-715(2) unless validly excluded.
Only an exclusion for personal injury from consumer goods is presumptively unconscionable.
topic: Tier 2 · Remedies & remedy limits (§§ 2-715, 2-718, 2-719) — Consequential exclusion survives (Razor)

q: Big Bird, a birdseed wholesaler, sells 1,000 sacks of seed that are stored at Snuffy's Storage, an independent warehouse. No document of title has been issued. At Big Bird's request, Snuffy's emails Cookie Monster: "We now hold the 1,000 sacks for you; come get them anytime." That evening, before Cookie Monster can arrange a truck, a fire at Snuffy's destroys the sacks. Who bears the loss?
o: Big Bird, because no document of title was ever issued.
Snuffy's, because a warehouse bears the risk of loss for goods it stores.
Big Bird, because Cookie Monster had no reasonable time to pick up the goods.
Big Bird, because a merchant seller keeps the risk until the buyer physically receives the goods.
Cookie Monster, because risk passed when the warehouse acknowledged his right to possession.
oe: A document isn't necessary. Acknowledgment by the bailee is one of the three ways risk passes under § 2-509(2).
A warehouse is liable only for its own failure of care. Between seller and buyer, the risk had passed.
The reasonable-time-to-present rule applies to a nonnegotiable document or a direction to the bailee. A bailee's acknowledgment passes risk right away.
The merchant receipt rule in § 2-509(3) doesn't govern goods held by a bailee. Section 2-509(2) does.

Correct. When goods are held by a bailee and are to be delivered without being moved, risk passes on the bailee's acknowledgment of the buyer's right to possession (§ 2-509(2)(b)). Snuffy's email was that acknowledgment.
topic: Tier 1 · Risk of loss & identification (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510) — Goods held by bailee; acknowledgment

q: Two merchants sign a contract containing a valid clause that any modification must be in a signed writing. The buyer later tells the seller by phone that it may deliver two weeks late. Relying on that call, the seller cancels a rush shipping arrangement that it can't reinstate. The buyer then insists on the original date. What is the most likely result?
o: The buyer wins, because when a contract has such a clause, a waiver must also be in writing.
The seller wins, because the phone call was a valid modification of the delivery date.
The buyer wins, because the no-oral-modification clause makes the phone call irrelevant.
The oral change can operate as a waiver, which the buyer likely can't retract now.
The seller wins, because no-oral-modification clauses can't be enforced between merchants.
oe: Article 2 imposes no such writing requirement for a waiver.
It wasn't a valid modification because of the clause. It works only as a waiver.
Section 2-209(4) gives the failed modification effect as a waiver.

Correct. An attempted modification that doesn't satisfy a no-oral-modification clause "can operate as a waiver" (§ 2-209(4)). A waiver can be retracted only if retraction wouldn't be unjust in view of a material change of position in reliance (§ 2-209(5)).
Between merchants, the clause is enforceable without a separate signature.
topic: Tier 2 · Modification (§ 2-209) — Failed modification as waiver

q: Best Car Rental rents cars by the day and week. Every four months, as a regular part of its business, it sells the oldest cars in its fleet to the public from a lot at its main office. Telly buys a two-year-old sedan from that lot. Nothing is said about warranties, and the transmission fails a week later in ordinary driving. Did Best Car Rental give an implied warranty of merchantability?
o: Yes, but only if the company knew about the transmission problem when it sold the car.
No, because the merchantability warranty doesn't apply to used cars sold at a low price.
No, because the company is in the rental business, not the business of selling cars.
Most likely yes, because it regularly sells used cars, so it deals in goods of that kind.
No, because the company never said anything to Telly about the car's mechanical condition.
oe: Implied warranty liability doesn't depend on the seller's knowledge.
Used goods sold by a merchant carry the warranty, adjusted for their age and condition.
A business can deal in goods of a kind even if selling them isn't its main line. Regular, scheduled sales from a sales lot are dealing.

Correct. The warranty arises when the seller is a merchant with respect to goods of that kind (§ 2-314(1)), meaning one who deals in them (§ 2-104(1)). A company that sells off its fleet on a regular schedule from a sales lot deals in used cars, unlike someone making an isolated sale. The warranty applies to used goods, measured by what's ordinary for a car of that age. See Problem 3-9(b).
The merchantability warranty is implied. No statement is needed.
topic: Tier 1 · Implied warranties (§§ 2-314, 2-315) — Fleet seller as merchant

q: In a regional livestock-auction trade, it is a long-standing and regularly observed practice that cattle sold at the ring carry no warranty against disease unless the auctioneer announces one. Rowlf, a rancher in that trade, buys cattle at auction. No warranty is announced and nothing is in writing. Several cattle turn out to have been sick at the time of sale. Can the seller rely on the trade usage to defeat Rowlf's merchantability claim?
o: No, because trade usage can supplement a contract but never take away rights.
Yes, but only if Rowlf actually knew of the usage.
Yes, because an implied warranty can be excluded or modified by usage of trade.
No, because a merchantability disclaimer must mention merchantability.
No, because any exclusion of an implied warranty must be in writing and conspicuous.
oe: Section 2-316(3)(c) expressly permits exclusion by trade usage.
A usage binds parties in the trade if they are or should be aware of it (§ 1-303(d)).
Correct. Section 2-316(3)(c) lets an implied warranty be excluded or modified by course of dealing, course of performance, or usage of trade, with no writing or particular words.
Section 2-316(2) is subject to § 2-316(3), which supplies alternative ways to exclude, including trade usage.
That's required only of a written merchantability disclaimer and of a fitness disclaimer, not of exclusion by trade usage.
topic: Tier 1 · Warranty disclaimers (§ 2-316) — Usage of trade excludes warranties

q: A grain dealer agrees to sell a miller 1,000 bushels of No. 2 yellow corn. The contract doesn't specify a source, and the dealer hasn't set aside any corn for the miller. A fire destroys the dealer's entire warehouse inventory. Is the dealer excused?
o: No, because the corn was never identified to the contract, and other corn is available.
Yes, because risk hadn't passed to the miller, so neither party owes anything for the lost corn.
No, but the miller must give the dealer a reasonable extra time to find replacement corn.
Yes, because losing its entire inventory makes the dealer's performance commercially impracticable.
Yes, because the fire destroyed the dealer's inventory without any fault on the dealer's part.
oe: Correct. Section 2-613 applies only to goods identified when the contract is made. When a seller can still meet a contract for fungible goods from other sources, the loss of its own stock isn't a casualty that excuses it.
The risk question asks who bears the loss of particular goods. The dealer still owes 1,000 bushels from somewhere.
Article 2 gives no automatic extension here.
Buying replacement corn may cost more, but increased cost alone doesn't make performance impracticable (§ 2-615 cmt. 4).
Lack of fault isn't enough. The goods must have been identified when the contract was made.
topic: Tier 2 · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-615) — Fungible goods not identified

q: Before selling a painting to Bert, a gallery owner tells him, "This artist is about to break out. This canvas will double in value within five years." Five years later, it's worth what Bert paid. Bert sues for breach of express warranty. What is the most likely result?
o: Bert wins, because the gallery is a merchant whose expertise in art Bert relied on.
The gallery wins, because a statement of the goods' value isn't a warranty.
Bert wins, because the gallery made a specific, measurable prediction about the canvas.
Bert wins, because express warranties can cover how goods will perform in the future.
The gallery wins, because the statement was made orally rather than in writing.
oe: Expertise can make some opinions into warranties, but a market-value prediction is excluded by statute.
Correct. "An affirmation merely of the value of the goods or a statement purporting to be merely the seller's opinion or commendation of the goods does not create a warranty" (§ 2-313(2)).
A prediction about market value is still an affirmation of value, and § 2-313(2) excludes it.
Warranties can cover performance of the goods themselves, but not their future market value.
Oral statements can be warranties. The problem is the content.
topic: Tier 1 · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Prediction of value

q: A fully integrated written contract with a merger clause, and no no-oral-modification clause, sets delivery for June 1. One week after signing, the parties orally agree to move delivery to June 15. The buyer later offers evidence of the oral agreement. Does the parol evidence rule bar it?
o: Yes, because the oral agreement contradicts the June 1 date stated in the writing.
No, because the rule doesn't reach agreements made after the writing.
No, but only if the oral agreement was supported by new consideration.
Yes, because any modification of a written sales contract must itself be in writing.
Yes, because the merger clause makes the written contract the only evidence of the deal.
oe: Contradiction matters only for prior or contemporaneous agreements.
Correct. Section 2-202 excludes evidence of "any prior agreement or of a contemporaneous oral agreement." A later agreement is a modification governed by § 2-209, not by the parol evidence rule.
Modifications need no consideration (§ 2-209(1)).
Without a no-oral-modification clause or a statute-of-frauds problem, an oral modification is effective (§ 2-209).
A merger clause speaks to prior and contemporaneous agreements, not to later changes.
topic: Tier 2 · Parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) — Later oral agreement isn't barred

q: A 12-month contract calls for monthly deliveries of 10,000 widgets by the 5th of each month. In April, May, and June the seller delivers on the 9th, and each time the buyer accepts without objection. In July, the seller again delivers on the 9th, and the buyer, without any earlier warning, rejects the shipment as late. What is the most likely result?
o: The rejection is proper, because a waiver of a contract term isn't binding without consideration.
The rejection is proper, because the written delivery date is an express term and controls over conduct.
The rejection is wrongful, because the contract has been permanently rewritten to require delivery by the 9th.
The rejection is proper, because a party who waives a term may retract the waiver at any time.
The rejection is likely wrongful, because the buyer had to give notice before demanding strict performance.
oe: A waiver needs no consideration.
Course of performance is relevant to show a waiver of an express term (§ 1-303(f)).
Waiver of an executory term can be retracted with reasonable notice. The more precise answer is that the buyer needed to give notice.
Retraction requires reasonable notice in advance and isn't allowed if it would be unjust because of a material change of position.

Correct. Repeated acceptance can show waiver or modification (§ 1-303(f)). A waiver affecting an executory part of the contract can be retracted only by "reasonable notification received by the other party that strict performance will be required" (§ 2-209(5)). The buyer gave none before July.
topic: Tier 2 · Course of performance, waiver & estoppel (§ 1-303) — Repeated waivers; retraction needs notice

q: Ernie buys a used tandem bicycle at a garage sale run by Bert, who had bought it in good faith from a stranger. It turns out the stranger stole it, and the true owner takes it back from Ernie. Ernie sues Bert. What is the most likely result?
o: Bert wins, because he sold the bike in good faith without knowing it had been stolen.
Bert wins, because by custom everything at a garage sale is sold "as is."
Ernie wins, because every seller warrants good title, whatever it knew.
Bert wins, because he isn't a merchant and was only selling his own used things.
Ernie wins, but only if he can show that Bert should have known the bike was stolen.
oe: Warranty liability doesn't depend on knowledge or fault.
"As is" doesn't exclude the title warranty. Only specific language or circumstances showing the seller doesn't claim title can (§ 2-312(2)).
Correct. Section 2-312(1) applies to every seller, merchant or not. The warranty is breached when the buyer doesn't get good title, and the seller's good faith is no defense.
The title warranty isn't limited to merchants.
No such showing is needed.
topic: Tier 1 · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-403) — Good-faith seller still breaches title warranty

q: On May 1, a seller delivers 50 industrial fans to a buyer. Delivery wasn't due until May 20. The fans are wired for 220 volts instead of the 110 volts the contract requires, which the seller could easily fix. The buyer emails, "We reject the fans as nonconforming," without saying why. On May 25, the buyer sues for breach. Can the buyer rely on the wiring defect?
o: Yes, because the seller should have inspected the fans before delivering them.
Yes, because the buyer gave the seller timely notice that it was rejecting the fans.
No, because a wiring problem doesn't substantially impair the value of the fans.
Yes, because under the perfect tender rule a buyer may reject for any defect at all.
No, because the buyer didn't state a defect the seller could have cured in time.
oe: The seller's diligence doesn't excuse the buyer's failure to particularize.
Notice of rejection is necessary but not sufficient. The defect must be stated when the seller could cure it.
Substantial impairment matters for installments and revocation, not a single-delivery rejection. The buyer's problem is § 2-605.
Perfect tender is subject to the seller's right to cure and to the duty to particularize.

Correct. A buyer's failure to state in connection with rejection a particular defect that is ascertainable by reasonable inspection bars reliance on it "where the seller could have cured it if stated seasonably" (§ 2-605(1)(a)). With time left before May 20, cure was possible (§ 2-508(1)).
topic: Tier 2 · Tender, inspection, acceptance & payment — Failure to particularize a curable defect

q: A seller of specialized medical gloves delegates its duty to supply a hospital to a little-known manufacturer that the hospital has never dealt with. The contract doesn't prohibit delegation, and the hospital has no substantial interest in the original seller's personal performance. What may the hospital do?
o: Demand adequate assurance from the new manufacturer, while keeping its rights against the seller.
Cancel the contract, because delegating performance to a stranger is a breach.
Demand assurance from the original seller, but never from the new manufacturer.
Nothing, because the delegation was permitted and the hospital has no substantial interest.
Refuse all deliveries until the original seller agrees in writing to remain liable.
oe: Correct. The other party "may treat any assignment which delegates performance as creating reasonable grounds for insecurity and may without prejudice to his rights against the assignor demand assurances from the assignee" (§ 2-210(6)).
A permitted delegation isn't a breach.
Section 2-210(6) expressly allows a demand on the assignee.
A permitted delegation still gives the hospital the right to demand assurance.
The original seller remains liable automatically under § 2-210(1).
topic: Tier 2 · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210) — Delegation as grounds for insecurity

q: Floyd orders 500 blue drum heads "for prompt shipment." The seller ships 500 white drum heads without any note or message. Has a contract been formed?
o: No, because the seller had to promise to ship before shipment could count as an acceptance.
No contract is formed until Floyd accepts the white drum heads by keeping or using them.
