Yes, but the seller isn't in breach, because Floyd can simply reject the white drum heads.
Yes, and the seller is in breach, because it shipped without saying the shipment was an accommodation.
No, because shipping goods that don't match the order is a counteroffer that Floyd may accept or reject.
oe: An order for prompt shipment may be accepted by either a promise to ship or shipment (§ 2-206(1)(b)).
The contract was formed when the seller shipped.
Being able to reject doesn't erase the breach.

Correct. An order for prompt shipment may be accepted by prompt shipment of conforming or nonconforming goods, "but such a shipment of non-conforming goods does not constitute an acceptance if the seller seasonably notifies the buyer that the shipment is offered only as an accommodation" (§ 2-206(1)(b)).
Under the UCC, it's an acceptance and a breach unless the seller sends an accommodation notice.
topic: Tier 3 · Formation, firm offers & § 2-207 — Shipment of nonconforming goods

q: Elmo buys a pressure cooker from a kitchen store. He lends it to his neighbor, Telly, who uses it in Telly's own kitchen. The lid explodes off and burns Telly. The state has adopted Alternative A of § 2-318. Can Telly sue the store for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability?
o: No, because only the person who bought the goods can ever sue for breach of warranty.
No, because Alternative A reaches only the buyer's family, household, and guests.
Yes, but only if the store knew that Elmo planned to lend the cooker to Telly.
Yes, because privity is never required for a personal-injury claim under Article 2.
Yes, because anyone who may reasonably be expected to use the goods may sue under Alternative A.
oe: Section 2-318 extends warranties to certain non-buyers. Telly just isn't in the protected group under Alternative A.

Correct. Alternative A covers "any natural person who is in the family or household of his buyer or who is a guest in his home" who may reasonably be expected to use, consume, or be affected by the goods and is injured in person. A neighbor using the cooker in his own home doesn't fit.
Alternative A doesn't turn on the seller's knowledge of a loan.
Section 2-318 defines how far privity is relaxed. Under Alternative A, Telly is outside it.
That broader reach is Alternative B. Alternative A is limited to family, household, and guests.
topic: Tier 1 · Implied warranties (§§ 2-314, 2-315) — Privity: § 2-318 Alternative A

q: Each of the following clauses appears in a sale contract. Which limitation is most likely unenforceable?
o: In a consumer toaster sale, a clause excluding consequential damages for personal injury.
In a consumer sale, a clause limiting the remedy to repair or replacement of defective parts.
In a merchant sale, a clause capping the seller's damages at the purchase price.
In a merchant sale of industrial equipment, a clause excluding liability for lost profits.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. "Limitation of consequential damages for injury to the person in the case of consumer goods is prima facie unconscionable" (§ 2-719(3)).
Repair-or-replace remedies are expressly permitted (§ 2-719(1)(a)).
Caps on damages are generally permitted between merchants.
A limitation where the loss is commercial isn't presumptively unconscionable (§ 2-719(3)).
One of the other choices is correct: In a consumer toaster sale, a clause excluding consequential damages for personal injury.
topic: Tier 2 · Remedies & remedy limits (§§ 2-715, 2-718, 2-719) — Consumer personal injury limitation

q: For six years, under a written supply agreement with no stated end date, Statler's Hardware has bought all its padlocks from Waldorf Locks. Waldorf abruptly stops shipping, with no notice, and tells Statler it is ending the relationship. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Waldorf has no liability, because a contract with no end date isn't enforceable at all.
Waldorf can't end the contract, because a six-year supply relationship becomes binding indefinitely.
Waldorf has no liability, because it ended the contract for a reason other than breach.
Waldorf is liable for all the profits Statler would have earned had the relationship continued.
Waldorf may end the deal but owed reasonable notice, so it's liable for the lack of notice.
oe: Indefinite-duration contracts are valid for a reasonable time (§ 2-309(2)).
Either party may terminate an indefinite contract on reasonable notice.
Termination for a reason other than breach still requires reasonable notice.
An indefinite contract can be terminated, so the buyer's damages are limited to the lack of notice.

Correct. A contract of indefinite duration "may be terminated at any time by either party" (§ 2-309(2)), but termination "requires that reasonable notification be received by the other party" (§ 2-309(3)). Courts limit damages to the harm from the missing notice, not the lost future of the relationship (as in Santa Fe Custom Shutters).
topic: Tier 3 · Termination & cancellation (§§ 2-106, 2-309) — Indefinite contract ended without notice

q: Herry sells 300 crates of pickles stored in Monster Cold Storage, an independent warehouse, to Prairie Dawn. At 2 p.m., Herry hands Prairie Dawn a signed letter addressed to the warehouse: "Please deliver the 300 crates to the bearer, Prairie Dawn." The warehouse hasn't been contacted. At 3 p.m., before Prairie Dawn could reasonably have reached the warehouse, an ammonia leak ruins the pickles. Who bears the loss?
o: Prairie Dawn, because receiving a signed direction to deliver completed Herry's tender.
The warehouse, because it had possession of the pickles when they were ruined.
Herry, because Prairie Dawn hadn't had a reasonable time to present the letter.
Prairie Dawn, because the warehouse would have honored the letter if she had arrived.
Prairie Dawn, because the pickles were identified and held by a bailee for her.
oe: Receipt of the direction alone isn't enough. The buyer also needs a reasonable time to present it.
The warehouse answers only for its own negligence. The question is which contracting party bears the loss.

Correct. Tender by a nonnegotiable document or a direction in a record to the bailee passes risk only after the buyer has had a reasonable time to present it (§§ 2-509(2)(c), 2-503(4)(b)). One hour wasn't enough.
The risk of the bailee's failure to honor, and the risk of loss, stay on the seller until a reasonable time to present has passed.
Goods held by a bailee are covered by § 2-509(2), and under subsection (2)(c) a direction passes risk only after a reasonable time.
topic: Tier 1 · Risk of loss & identification (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510) — Direction to bailee; reasonable time to present

q: Beaker buys a $40,000 centrifuge from Muppet Labs Supply. After using it for a month, he discovers a hidden defect that substantially impairs its value and rightfully revokes his acceptance. While he waits for the seller to pick it up, a fire in Beaker's lab destroys it without his fault. Beaker's own insurance pays $25,000 for the loss. How much of the loss does the seller bear?
o: Nothing, because Beaker's insurer must bear the whole loss.
$15,000, the part of the loss Beaker's insurance doesn't cover.
$40,000, because a rightful revocation puts the entire risk back on the seller.
Nothing, because the centrifuge was in Beaker's lab and he had accepted it.
$20,000, because the loss is split evenly once the buyer revokes.
oe: The seller still bears whatever the buyer's insurance doesn't cover.

Correct. When the buyer rightfully revokes acceptance, it may treat the risk as having rested on the seller from the beginning, but only "to the extent of any deficiency in his effective insurance coverage" (§ 2-510(2)). Beaker's insurer covers $25,000, so the seller bears the $15,000 shortfall.
Section 2-510(2) limits the seller's risk to the shortfall in the buyer's insurance.
Acceptance was revoked, and § 2-510(2) treats the risk as having rested on the seller from the beginning.
There is no even split. The allocation turns on the buyer's insurance coverage.
topic: Tier 1 · Risk of loss & identification (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510) — Revocation of acceptance; insurance deficiency

q: When Abby asks about a used car's history, the private seller replies, "It's never been in an accident." Abby buys it. In fact it had been in a serious crash. The seller raises three defenses: (1) the statement was oral; (2) the seller didn't intend to make a warranty and never used the word "guarantee"; and (3) Abby could have discovered the truth by having a mechanic inspect the car. Which defense, if any, is valid?
o: Defense (1) only.
Defense (2) only.
Defense (3) only.
Defenses (2) and (3).
None of the above.
oe: Express warranties don't have to be written. Oral affirmations of fact can be the basis of the bargain.
Section 2-313(2) says formal words like "warrant" or "guarantee" aren't needed, and neither is a specific intention to make a warranty.
A buyer's opportunity to inspect doesn't defeat an express warranty.
Neither defense is valid.

Correct. None of the defenses is valid. An oral, specific affirmation of fact given in response to the buyer's question can be part of the basis of the bargain (§ 2-313(1)(a)). No formal words or intent are required (§ 2-313(2)), and a buyer who could have inspected but relied on the seller's statement keeps the warranty.
topic: Tier 1 · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Seller's three defenses to an express warranty

q: After a seller's third late and defective delivery under an installment contract, which substantially impairs the value of the whole contract, the buyer writes: "We hereby terminate our agreement effective immediately." Two months later, the buyer sues for damages for the seller's breaches. The seller argues that by "terminating" the contract the buyer gave up its claims. What is the most likely result?
o: The buyer keeps its claim only if its letter expressly reserved its rights to sue for damages.
The seller wins, because termination discharges all of both parties' obligations under the contract.
The buyer keeps its claim, because ending a contract for breach preserves remedies for the breach.
The buyer keeps its claim, but only for the third delivery, which was the one that ended the contract.
The seller wins, because the buyer chose to "terminate" the agreement rather than to cancel it.
oe: No express reservation is required (§ 2-720).
Even on termination, rights based on prior breach or performance survive (§ 2-106(3)).

Correct. Putting an end to a contract "by reason of breach by the other" is cancellation, and "the cancelling party also retains any remedy for breach of the whole contract or any unperformed balance" (§ 2-106(4)). The label the buyer used doesn't control, and words of termination aren't read as a renunciation of damages claims unless that intention clearly appears (§ 2-720).
A cancellation for breach of the whole contract preserves remedies for the whole contract.
Article 2 looks at the reason the contract ended, not the word used.
topic: Tier 3 · Termination & cancellation (§§ 2-106, 2-309) — Ending for breach keeps the damages claim

q: Under a contract requiring delivery of 400 lamps by June 30, a seller delivers on June 10, but 40 of the lamps have cracked shades. The buyer rightfully rejects. The seller immediately notifies the buyer that it will deliver 400 conforming lamps by June 25, and it does. Must the buyer accept them?
o: No, because the buyer's rightful rejection of the first delivery ended the contract.
No, because a seller may cure only if it reasonably believed the first tender would be accepted.
Yes, because the seller notified the buyer and cured within the contract time.
Yes, but only if the buyer agrees in writing to let the seller make a second delivery.
No, because after a rightful rejection the buyer may cover elsewhere instead.
oe: A rightful rejection doesn't cut off the seller's right to cure within the contract period.
That condition applies to cure after the contract time expires (§ 2-508(2)), not before.

Correct. When a tender is rejected as nonconforming and the time for performance hasn't expired, the seller may seasonably notify the buyer of its intention to cure and then make a conforming delivery within the contract time (§ 2-508(1)).
Cure under § 2-508(1) doesn't require the buyer's consent.
The buyer can't cover in place of a timely, proper cure. There's no uncured breach.
topic: Tier 2 · Tender, inspection, acceptance & payment — Cure before the contract time expires

q: At a sheriff's execution sale held to satisfy a court judgment against a debtor, Gonzo buys a motorcycle that the sheriff had seized from the debtor's garage. Nothing is said about title. It turns out the motorcycle belonged to the debtor's neighbor, who reclaims it. Gonzo sues the sheriff for breach of the warranty of title. What is the most likely result?
o: Gonzo wins, because the sheriff never said the motorcycle was sold "as is."
Gonzo wins, because the neighbor never entrusted the motorcycle to anyone.
Gonzo loses, because the motorcycle was used and used goods carry no title warranty.
Gonzo loses, because the nature of a sheriff's sale disclaims the title warranty.
Gonzo wins, because every seller warrants good title unless it uses specific disclaimer language.
oe: "As is" wouldn't exclude title anyway. Here the circumstances do.
Entrustment would matter in a contest between Gonzo and the neighbor. The question is whether the sheriff gave a title warranty.
Used goods carry the title warranty. The result turns on the nature of the sale.

Correct. The title warranty can be excluded "by circumstances which give the buyer reason to know that the person selling does not claim title in himself or that he is purporting to sell only such right or title as he or a third person may have" (§ 2-312(2)). Comment 5 lists sheriffs, executors, and foreclosing lienors. See Problem 5-5(b).
Specific language is one way to exclude the warranty. Circumstances are the other.
topic: Tier 1 · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-403) — Sheriff's sale: title disclaimed by circumstances

q: Fisk buys a used car from Lonborg. Before signing, Lonborg tells him, "It's never been in an accident." The signed sales contract, which is complete and exclusive, says: "Sold AS IS. Seller makes no warranty, express or implied." Fisk later learns the car was badly damaged in a prior crash. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The rule likely bars the oral warranty, but Fisk may still use the statement to prove fraud.
Fisk has no remedy at all, because he signed a contract that said "as is."
The oral warranty controls, because express warranties always prevail over disclaimers.
The oral statement is admissible as a consistent additional term of the agreement.
The "as is" clause is ineffective, because it didn't specifically mention merchantability.
oe: Correct. A prior oral warranty that contradicts a complete written disclaimer is excluded by § 2-202, and § 2-316(1) makes its express-warranty rule subject to the parol evidence rule. Evidence offered to prove fraud isn't barred, because the rule doesn't displace the law of fraud (§ 1-103(b)). See Problem 5-13.
The parol evidence rule doesn't bar a fraud claim.
Under § 2-316(1), that preference is "subject to the provisions of this Article on parol or extrinsic evidence."
It contradicts "Seller makes no warranty, express or implied," and the writing is complete and exclusive.
"As is" doesn't need to mention merchantability (§ 2-316(3)(a)), and in any event the parol evidence question turns on the writing's integration, not on the disclaimer's wording.
topic: Tier 2 · Parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) — Oral warranty vs. "as is" writing

q: Fozzie agrees to buy all the bolts his widget plant requires from Kermit at a fixed price. The contract estimates 90,000 bolts a year, and Fozzie bought 90,000 in year one and 100,000 in year two. In year three, a huge new customer contract triples Fozzie's legitimate need, and he demands 300,000 bolts. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Kermit must supply 300,000 bolts, but may charge the market price for the excess.
Kermit need supply only an amount not unreasonably disproportionate to the estimate.
Kermit must supply all 300,000 bolts, because Fozzie's increased need is in good faith.
The contract is unenforceable, because it never stated a definite quantity of bolts.
Kermit may cancel the whole contract because the demand is so far above the estimate.
oe: Article 2 doesn't reprice the disproportionate excess. Kermit simply isn't obligated to supply it.

Correct. A requirements quantity must be in good faith, and "no quantity unreasonably disproportionate to any stated estimate or in the absence of a stated estimate to any normal or otherwise comparable prior output or requirements may be tendered or demanded" (§ 2-306(1)). Good faith alone doesn't satisfy both limits. See Problem 4-2.
Good faith is necessary but not sufficient. The disproportion limit is separate.
Requirements contracts are enforceable (§ 2-306(1)).
A disproportionate demand doesn't let the seller cancel. It need only supply a reasonable quantity.
topic: Tier 2 · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Requirements: good faith but disproportionate

q: Under a two-year contract for monthly shipments of printer paper, payment is due on the 1st of each month. For the first eight months, the buyer pays on the 10th, and the seller cashes every check without objecting. What best describes the pattern of late payments?
o: An express term of the contract.
A modification that requires a signed writing.
A course of dealing.
A usage of trade.
A course of performance.
oe: Express terms are what the parties stated, not their later conduct.
Conduct can show waiver or modification, and § 2-209 needs no writing unless a clause or the statute of frauds requires one. In any event the pattern itself is a course of performance.
A course of dealing concerns conduct in previous transactions between the parties (§ 1-303(b)), not repeated performance under this contract.
A usage of trade is a practice regularly observed in a trade or place (§ 1-303(c)), not the parties' own conduct.

Correct. A course of performance is a sequence of conduct between the parties to a particular transaction that involves repeated occasions for performance, which the other party accepted or acquiesced in without objection (§ 1-303(a)).
topic: Tier 2 · Course of performance, waiver & estoppel (§ 1-303) — Identifying a course of performance

q: On March 1, Scooter orders a sound mixer by phone, and the store agrees to sell it. The mixer arrives on March 10 in a box with a printed card inside: "SELLER DISCLAIMS ALL IMPLIED WARRANTIES, INCLUDING MERCHANTABILITY." Scooter never signs or agrees to anything else. The mixer fails in ordinary use. Is the disclaimer effective?
o: Yes, because the card mentions merchantability and is printed in capital letters.
Yes, because a modification of a sales contract needs no consideration under § 2-209.
Yes, because by keeping the mixer, Scooter assented to the terms on the card.
No, because merchantability can never be disclaimed in a sale to a consumer.
No, because it came after the contract was formed and Scooter never agreed to it.
oe: It meets the form requirements of § 2-316(2), but it never became part of the deal.
A modification needs no consideration, but it does need agreement.
Keeping goods bought under an existing contract doesn't show assent to new terms.
Article 2 allows consumer disclaimers that meet § 2-316. The problem here is timing.
Correct. A disclaimer is effective only if it's part of the contract. Terms delivered after formation are at most a proposal to modify, which needs the buyer's assent (§ 2-209). See Problem 5-4.
topic: Tier 1 · Warranty disclaimers (§ 2-316) — Disclaimer delivered with the goods

q: A restaurant buys a commercial dishwasher. The seller knew the restaurant had no backup machine. The dishwasher breaks down because of a defect. Which of the following losses is a consequential damage rather than an incidental one?
o: The cost of storing the dishwasher while waiting for the seller to pick it up.
The commission paid to a broker to find a replacement dishwasher quickly.
The cost of having a technician inspect the dishwasher to confirm the defect.
Profits lost while the restaurant was closed for two days.
The cost of shipping the broken dishwasher back to the seller.
oe: Expenses of care and custody of rejected goods are incidental (§ 2-715(1)).
Commercially reasonable charges in effecting cover are incidental (§ 2-715(1)).
Reasonable inspection expenses are incidental damages (§ 2-715(1)).

Correct. Consequential damages include losses from the buyer's general or particular requirements that the seller had reason to know of when contracting and that the buyer couldn't reasonably prevent (§ 2-715(2)(a)).
Transportation expenses after a breach are incidental (§ 2-715(1)).
topic: Tier 2 · Remedies & remedy limits (§§ 2-715, 2-718, 2-719) — Incidental vs. consequential damages

q: A steel fabricator contracts to deliver 500 tons of rebar at a fixed price. Before delivery, ordinary market forces drive the price of scrap steel up 40%, which turns the expected profit into a loss. The fabricator argues it is excused under § 2-615. What is the most likely result?
o: Not excused, because § 2-615 applies only to buyers, never to sellers.
Excused, as long as the fabricator gives the buyer seasonable notice of the problem.
Excused, but only for the part of the order it can no longer afford to fill.
Not excused, because a rise in cost alone doesn't make performance impracticable.
Excused, because a 40% jump in the cost of scrap steel makes performance commercially impracticable.
oe: Section 2-615 is written for sellers.
Notice is required for excuse but doesn't create excuse.
Partial excuse requires an excusing contingency that affects capacity, not just higher cost.

Correct. "Increased cost alone does not excuse performance unless the rise in cost is due to some unforeseen contingency which alters the essential nature of the performance" (§ 2-615 cmt. 4). Market fluctuation is exactly the risk a fixed-price contract allocates.
A market increase is a foreseeable business risk, not an unforeseen contingency.
topic: Tier 2 · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-615) — Cost increase isn't impracticability

q: Directed Decorating locates antique furniture for luxury hotels. It introduces the hotel to the antique's owner, the owner sells directly to the hotel, and the hotel pays Directed Decorating a finder's fee. A chair it located collapses because of rot that was present when it was sold. Is Directed Decorating liable for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability?
o: Yes, because it holds itself out as having special knowledge and skill regarding antiques.
No, because Directed Decorating only located the chair and never sold it to the hotel.
No, because antiques are used goods, and used goods carry no implied warranties.
Yes, because it received money in the transaction in the form of a finder's fee.
Yes, but only if the chair's owner who sold it was not a merchant.
oe: Knowledge or skill can make someone a merchant, but merchantability still requires that person to be the seller.

Correct. Section 2-314(1) implies the warranty in a contract for sale by a seller who is a merchant. A finder or broker that never sells the goods doesn't make the warranty, though the actual seller might. See Problem 3-9(d).
Used goods can carry the warranty when sold by a merchant seller. The problem here is that Directed Decorating sold nothing.
A finder's fee from the buyer doesn't make the finder a seller.
Liability doesn't shift to the finder because the actual seller isn't a merchant.
topic: Tier 1 · Implied warranties (§§ 2-314, 2-315) — Finder isn't a seller

q: A buyer prepays the full $50,000 price for custom shelving. The contract says, "Neither party may assign any right under this contract." Before delivery, the buyer sells its business and assigns its right to receive the shelving to the new owner. The seller refuses to deliver to the new owner. What is the most likely result?
o: Effective, but only if the seller consents, because the contract contains an anti-assignment clause.
Ineffective, because the contract expressly prohibits either party from assigning any right.
Effective despite the clause, because the buyer has fully performed its side of the contract.
Ineffective, because a right to receive goods, unlike a right to payment, can never be assigned.
The assignment breaches the contract, so the seller may keep the price and refuse to deliver.
oe: Consent isn't required when the exception applies.
The full-performance exception in § 2-210(2) overrides the clause.

Correct. Under § 2-210(2), "a right to damages for breach of the whole contract or a right arising out of the assignor's due performance of his entire obligation can be assigned despite agreement otherwise." Having paid in full, the buyer has fully performed.
Rights to goods can be assigned, subject to § 2-210(2)'s limits.
Because the exception applies, the assignment is effective and the seller must deliver.
topic: Tier 2 · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210) — Assignment after full performance

q: Under § 2-314(2), which of the following is NOT one of the standards goods must meet to be merchantable?
o: They must be of the highest quality the seller offers in that line of goods.
Within the variations the agreement allows, they must be of even kind, quality, and quantity within each unit and among all units.
They must be adequately contained, packaged, and labeled as the agreement may require.
They must conform to any promises or affirmations of fact on the container or label.
They must pass without objection in the trade under the contract description.
oe: Correct. Merchantability is a floor, not a promise of top quality. The goods need only meet the minimum standards in § 2-314(2).
topic: Tier 1 · Implied warranties (§§ 2-314, 2-315) — Merchantable: which is NOT a standard

q: A buyer's purchase order for 3,000 yards of fabric states: "Acceptance is expressly limited to the terms of this order." The seller's acknowledgment, which doesn't make its acceptance conditional, adds a minor term that wouldn't materially alter the deal: "Seller may ship in rolls of 50 to 60 yards." Both parties are merchants, and the buyer never responds. Is the roll-size term part of the contract?
o: No, because the buyer's purchase order expressly limited acceptance to the terms of the order.
No contract was formed, because the seller's acknowledgment didn't mirror the purchase order.
Yes, because the seller's acknowledgment was the last form exchanged before performance.
Yes, because the buyer received the acknowledgment and never objected to the new term.
Yes, because the roll-size term is minor and wouldn't materially alter the parties' deal.
oe: Correct. The acknowledgment is still an acceptance under § 2-207(1), but between merchants an additional term becomes part of the contract only if none of the § 2-207(2) exceptions applies, and the first exception is that "the offer expressly limits acceptance to the terms of the offer."
Section 2-207(1) rejects the mirror-image rule.
Article 2 rejects the last-shot rule.
Objection is a separate exception. The limiting language already excludes the term.
Lack of material alteration is only one requirement. The offer's limiting language independently keeps the term out.
topic: Tier 3 · Formation, firm offers & § 2-207 — Offer expressly limits acceptance to its terms

q: A buyer's purchase order includes a warranty term. The seller's acknowledgment says: "Our acceptance is expressly conditional on your assent to our terms," and its terms include a disclaimer. The buyer never assents to the seller's terms, but the seller ships and the buyer pays. A dispute arises over warranties. Under § 2-207, what are the terms of the contract?
o: The buyer's terms, because its purchase order was the offer.
The seller's terms, because the buyer accepted them by paying for the goods.
The terms on which the writings agree, plus Article 2's gap fillers.
Whatever terms the court finds most reasonable under the circumstances.
There's no contract, because the writings didn't form one.
oe: Under § 2-207(3), neither party's form controls where they differ.
Paying after an expressly conditional response isn't assent to the seller's terms. Section 2-207(3) applies.

Correct. An expressly conditional acceptance isn't an acceptance under § 2-207(1). The parties' conduct then establishes a contract under § 2-207(3), whose terms are those "on which the writings of the parties agree, together with any supplementary terms incorporated under any other provisions of this Act," including the implied warranties.
Section 2-207(3) supplies the formula: the agreed terms plus Article 2's gap fillers.
Conduct recognizing the existence of a contract establishes one (§ 2-207(3)).
topic: Tier 3 · Formation, firm offers & § 2-207 — Expressly conditional acceptance, then performance

q: At a trade show, Mahna Mahna Industries displays a model of a commercial ice machine. The model was built for the show, not taken from production stock. Its tag reads "500 lb/day." Pepe orders ten machines "same as the display model." The machines delivered produce 300 lb/day and use a cheaper compressor than the model. Which statement is most accurate?
o: No warranty arose, because trade-show displays are advertising, not part of the bargain.
The model and its tag created express warranties that the machines would match them.
The tag created a warranty, but the model itself created none because it wasn't for sale.
No warranty arose, because Pepe saw the model and could judge its quality for himself.
No warranty arose, because only samples drawn from the actual goods create warranties.
oe: Displays can create warranties when the buyer orders by reference to them.

Correct. A model made part of the basis of the bargain creates an express warranty that the goods will conform (§ 2-313(1)(c)). A model not drawn from the bulk may carry less weight than a true sample (§ 2-313 cmt. 6), but ordering "same as the display model" makes it part of the bargain, and the tag is a specific affirmation.
Both the tag and the model are part of the bargain.
Inspecting a model is how a warranty by model is formed, not a defense to one.
Section 2-313(1)(c) covers both samples and models.
topic: Tier 1 · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Model at a trade show

q: A contract for 2,000 coffee mugs is "F.O.B. Seller's plant" and says nothing about when payment is due. The seller ships the mugs and demands payment on the day of shipment. The buyer says it will pay when the mugs arrive. Who is right?
o: Neither; payment is due within a reasonable time after shipment.
The buyer, but only if it has already inspected the mugs.
The seller, because risk passed on shipment, so payment is due then too.
The seller, because under an F.O.B. shipment term delivery occurs at the seller's plant.
None of the above.
oe: Section 2-310(a) ties payment to receipt, not to a reasonable time.
Payment is due on receipt, and inspection rights are a separate matter under § 2-513.
Risk and payment are separate questions under §§ 2-509 and 2-310.
The F.O.B. term governs delivery and risk, not when payment is due.

Correct. The buyer is right, but not for any reason listed. Unless otherwise agreed, payment is due "at the time and place at which the buyer is to receive the goods even though the place of shipment is the place of delivery" (§ 2-310(a)). The buyer's separate right to inspect under § 2-513 is not a condition of that rule.
topic: Tier 2 · Tender, inspection, acceptance & payment — Payment due on receipt despite shipment term

q: At Pepe's Cantina, Rizzo orders a "shredded chicken enchilada" and breaks a tooth on a one-inch chicken bone in the filling. Rizzo sues for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Rizzo wins under any test, because food that injures a diner isn't fit for the ordinary purpose of being eaten.
Rizzo wins, but only if he proves that Pepe's kitchen staff failed to use reasonable care in preparing the filling.
Pepe's wins, because a restaurant can't be liable for a hidden bone that it didn't know about and couldn't have found.
It depends on the test: a natural bone defeats the claim under the foreign-natural test, but not necessarily under the reasonable-expectation test.
Pepe's wins under any test, because a meal served in a restaurant is a sale of services, which Article 2 doesn't cover.
oe: The foreign-natural test could defeat the claim, and even the reasonable-expectation test turns on the facts.
Warranty liability doesn't require negligence.
Implied warranty liability is strict. The seller's knowledge is irrelevant.

Correct. Serving food for value is a sale (§ 2-314(1)). Courts that use the older foreign-natural test deny recovery for natural substances. Most courts now ask what a consumer would reasonably expect, which for a shredded filling likely favors Rizzo.
Section 2-314(1) expressly treats serving food or drink for value as a sale.
topic: Tier 1 · Implied warranties (§§ 2-314, 2-315) — Food: foreign-natural vs. reasonable expectation

q: A seller agreed to deliver equipment with payment due 15 days after delivery. Before the next shipment, the seller learns that the buyer's credit rating has been cut, that other suppliers aren't being paid on time, and that the buyer has changed banks. The seller sends a signed letter demanding adequate assurance and suspends shipment. The buyer doesn't respond for 35 days. What may the seller do?
o: Treat the buyer's silence as a repudiation only after 90 days.
Nothing more; it must resume shipping and wait to see whether the buyer pays.
Sue the buyer for the full price of all future shipments.
Treat the buyer's failure to respond as a repudiation of the contract.
None of the above.
oe: The statutory limit is 30 days.
After 30 days without adequate assurance, the seller may treat the contract as repudiated.
Repudiation opens the seller's remedies, but the price is generally recoverable only for goods accepted or in limited cases (§ 2-709).

Correct. With reasonable grounds for insecurity, a party may demand adequate assurance in a record and suspend its own performance. Failure to provide assurance within a reasonable time not exceeding 30 days after receiving a justified demand is a repudiation (§ 2-609(1), (4)). See Problem 6-3.
One of the other choices is correct: Treat the buyer's failure to respond as a repudiation of the contract.
topic: Tier 2 · Insecurity & repudiation (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Silence after a justified demand

q: A bakery agrees to buy all the eggs it requires for its custard line from a farm, with an estimate of 2,000 dozen a month. Facing declining custard sales and for sound business reasons unrelated to the egg contract, the bakery discontinues the custard line, and its requirements drop to zero. The farm sues. Under the approach most courts take, what is the most likely result?
o: The farm wins, because a requirements buyer must take at least the estimated quantity.
The farm wins, because any drop far below the estimate is unreasonably disproportionate.
The bakery likely wins, because a reduction made in good faith for business reasons isn't a breach.
The bakery wins only if it gave the farm a year's notice before discontinuing the line.
The contract was never enforceable, because requirements contracts lack mutuality.
oe: An estimate isn't a minimum, though it bears on what is disproportionate.
Most courts don't apply the disproportion limit that strictly to good-faith decreases.

Correct. Most courts read § 2-306(1)'s disproportion limit mainly as a check on increases and judge reductions by good faith. A buyer that cuts its requirements for legitimate business reasons, rather than to escape a bad bargain, doesn't breach (see § 2-306 cmt. 2).
Section 2-306 has no fixed notice period. The test is good faith.
Section 2-306 and good faith supply the needed mutuality.
topic: Tier 2 · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Requirements: good-faith drop to near zero

q: Sam Eagle's bottling plant gives Gonzo's Pump Works a 30-page specification for a custom pump: flow rate, materials, seals, and motor size. Gonzo builds the pump exactly to those specifications. In service, the pump can't keep up with the plant's actual line speed. Sam sues for breach of the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose. What is the most likely result?
o: Sam wins, because Gonzo knew the pump would be used in a bottling plant.
Gonzo wins, because the fitness warranty never applies to specially manufactured goods.
Sam wins, because a pump that can't keep up with the line isn't merchantable.
Sam wins, because Gonzo is a merchant that deals in pumps and so warrants their fitness.
Gonzo wins, because Sam relied on his own specifications, not on Gonzo's judgment.
oe: Knowledge of the purpose is only half the test. Reliance on the seller is also required.
Specially manufactured goods can carry a fitness warranty when the buyer relies on the seller's design.
A pump built to the buyer's specifications that works as specified is likely fit for its ordinary purpose. The shortfall came from the specifications.
Merchant status matters for merchantability, not for fitness.

Correct. The fitness warranty requires that the buyer rely on the seller's skill or judgment to select or furnish suitable goods (§ 2-315). A buyer that dictates detailed specifications usually relies on its own judgment, not the seller's.
topic: Tier 1 · Implied warranties (§§ 2-314, 2-315) — Buyer's own specifications defeat reliance

q: Sam Eagle, new to the lumber business, orders 5,000 "2x4" studs from a mill. The studs delivered measure 1.5 by 3.5 inches. In the lumber trade, "2x4" universally refers to that finished size. Sam claims he expected boards a full 2 by 4 inches and had never heard of the trade practice. What is the most likely result?
o: The trade meaning controls, because a trade usage binds those engaged in the trade.
Sam wins, because the plain, literal words of the written order control over custom.
Sam wins, because a usage of trade binds a party only if he actually knew of it.
The mill wins only if it can show a prior course of dealing with Sam in the same goods.
The mill wins only if the trade meaning of "2x4" was written into the contract.
oe: Correct. A usage of trade in the vocation or trade in which the parties are engaged, or of which they are or should be aware, gives meaning to and supplements their agreement (§ 1-303(d)).
Article 2 reads words in light of trade usage. A literal reading doesn't prevail over an established trade meaning.
The test includes parties who are engaged in the trade or should be aware of the usage.
Usage of trade works independently of any course of dealing.
Usage of trade supplements the contract without being stated.
topic: Tier 2 · Course of performance, waiver & estoppel (§ 1-303) — Usage binds a newcomer to the trade

q: A five-year supply contract provides: "This agreement ends automatically if Buyer closes its Wilmington store." The buyer closes that store, and the contract ends. The seller argues the buyer had to give it reasonable notice first. Is the seller right?
o: Yes, because any agreement that dispenses with notice of termination is invalid.
No, because no notice is needed when the contract ends on an agreed event.
Yes, because the duty of good faith requires the buyer to warn the seller first.
No, because closing the store was a breach, so the seller canceled the contract.
Yes, because every termination of a sales contract requires reasonable notice.
oe: A clause dispensing with notice is invalid only if its operation would be unconscionable.

Correct. Termination "except on the happening of an agreed event" requires reasonable notification (§ 2-309(3)). When the parties agree that a specified event ends the contract, no notice is required.
Good faith applies, but it doesn't add a notice requirement that the statute excepts.
Closing the store was the agreed ending event, not a breach.
Section 2-309(3) expressly excepts termination on an agreed event.
topic: Tier 3 · Termination & cancellation (§§ 2-106, 2-309) — Termination on an agreed event

q: Which statement most accurately distinguishes a merger clause from a no-oral-modification clause?
o: A merger clause makes a contract enforceable under the statute of frauds, and a no-oral-modification clause doesn't.
A no-oral-modification clause keeps out evidence of usage of trade; a merger clause doesn't.
Both clauses do the same work, so a well-drafted contract needs only one of them.
A merger clause deals with later changes; a no-oral-modification clause deals with earlier agreements.
A merger clause deals with earlier agreements; a no-oral-modification clause, with later ones.

q: Rizzo's Manufacturing builds 10,000 novelty umbrellas to a design and specifications furnished by Pepe's Party Supply. A patent holder sues both companies, claiming the umbrella design infringes its patent. As between Rizzo's and Pepe's, who bears the infringement claim?
o: They split it equally, because both companies took part in making the umbrellas.
Pepe's, because a buyer that furnishes the specifications must hold the seller harmless.
Rizzo's, because the warranty of title protects the buyer against patent claims.
Rizzo's, because a merchant manufacturer always warrants that its goods don't infringe.
Neither, until a court decides whether the patent holder's patent is valid.
oe: Section 2-312(3) puts this claim entirely on the buyer.

Correct. A merchant seller regularly dealing in goods of the kind warrants against infringement, "but a buyer who furnishes specifications to the seller must hold the seller harmless against any such claim which arises out of compliance with the specifications" (§ 2-312(3)).
The title warranty concerns ownership and liens, not patents.
The warranty against infringement doesn't cover claims arising from the buyer's own specifications.
Allocation between the parties doesn't wait for a ruling on the patent's validity.

q: A seller repudiates a contract to sell 1,000 office chairs at $100 each. The buyer promptly and reasonably buys 1,000 comparable chairs from another supplier at $130 each. The market price at the time the buyer learned of the repudiation was $125. The buyer also spent $200 on reasonable costs of finding the substitute chairs, and it saved no expenses because of the breach. If the buyer sues for damages based on cover, how much does it recover?
oe: Correct. A buyer that covers may recover the difference between the cost of cover and the contract price, plus incidental and consequential damages, less expenses saved (§ 2-712(2)). That's ($130 - $100) x 1,000 = $30,000, plus $200 in incidental damages (§ 2-715(1)).
That uses the market price under § 2-713. A buyer that has reasonably covered measures damages by the cover price.
The buyer recovers the difference between cover and contract price, not the whole cost of cover.
This uses the market measure and also omits incidental damages.
This leaves out the $200 of incidental damages, which a covering buyer may recover.
topic: Tier 2 · Remedies & remedy limits (§§ 2-715, 2-718, 2-719) — Buyer's cover damages

q: A buyer's purchase order for 1,000 valves says nothing about warranties. Both parties are merchants, and neither objects. The valves leak. Is merchantability disclaimed?
o: No, because a warranty disclaimer materially alters the deal, so it isn't part of it.
Yes, because between merchants an additional term is part of the contract unless the buyer objects.
Yes, because the seller's acknowledgment was the last form sent before performance.
Yes, because the clause mentions merchantability and is conspicuous, as § 2-316 requires.

Two days later, while the seller is arranging to resell, a burst pipe ruins the pots. The seller's insurer pays 70% of their value. What is the most likely result?
o: The restaurant bears the entire loss, because a breaching party bears all risk of loss.
The seller bears the entire loss, because the pots were destroyed before the June 1 pickup.
The seller may treat the uninsured 30% of the loss as resting on the restaurant.

q: A drought cuts a cranberry grower's harvest in half. Cranberries from its own bogs are the agreed source in several contracts, and it also has regular customers who buy without contracts. Which statement about the grower's duties is most accurate?
o: It may choose which contract buyers to supply in full and which contracts to cancel outright.
It must buy cranberries from other growers to fill every contract in full at the contract price.
It must fill its contract orders in full before it sells any berries to customers without contracts.
It must allocate fairly, may include regular non-contract customers, and must notify buyers.
It is excused from all its contracts, because the drought was an unforeseen contingency.
oe: Allocation must be fair and reasonable.
Where the parties agreed that the berries would come from the grower's own bogs, failure of that source can excuse the shortfall (§ 2-615 cmt. 5).
Section 2-615(b) permits including regular customers not under contract in the allocation.

Correct. When a contingency affects only part of a seller's capacity, the seller must allocate production and deliveries among its customers fairly and reasonably, may include regular customers not then under contract, and must notify buyers seasonably (§ 2-615(b), (c)).
A partial failure calls for allocation, not complete excuse.
